10815-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled the Messages and Papers of the Presidents by authority of Congress, and this fourth volume covers March 4, 1841, to March 4, 1849. It holds the terms of Harrison and Tyler and the term of James K. Polk. The death of President Harrison, the first time a vice-president succeeded under the Constitution, opens the period, with papers on his death included.

Tyler's vetoes, including two against bills chartering a national bank, appear among the documents. The volume is a primary source for the age of expansion and party strife. Readers and researchers get the presidents' own words, in official form, for eight crowded years.
10858-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation turns to Andrew Jackson in this volume, covering his first term from March 4, 1829, to March 4, 1833. A short life opens it: Jackson was born in the Waxhaw settlement in 1767, son of an Irish immigrant who died the year he was born. Captured by the British in 1781 and wounded for refusing to clean an officer's boots, he studied law at Salisbury and moved to Nashville.

The volume then prints Jackson's messages and proclamations, the record of a turbulent presidency. Richardson's series preserves the official papers in order. Readers get Jackson's public voice, framed by the hard youth that made him.
10879-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson gathered the official papers of John Quincy Adams in this volume of his presidential series. A short life sketch opens the book, tracing Adams from his boyhood travels in Europe through Harvard, the law, and diplomatic posts in Holland, Prussia, and Russia. It then presents the documents of his presidency, in the order the administration issued them.

Readers get the presidency in its own words: messages to Congress, proclamations, and papers on foreign affairs and public finance. The volume shows how Adams explained his policies and answered Congress, and it preserves the record of a single administration for later study. Students of the early republic can follow debates over trade, debt, and the nation's place abroad without relying on secondhand summaries.
10893-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's series reaches Thomas Jefferson in this volume, covering March 1801 to March 1809. A life sketch follows Jefferson from Shadwell, Virginia, through William and Mary, the law, and the Virginia legislature to the Continental Congress, where he drafted the Declaration of Independence. Diplomatic service in France and the office of Secretary of State come before the presidency.

Jefferson's own papers follow: messages to Congress, proclamations, and documents on the Louisiana Purchase, relations with France and Spain, and disputes over trade and western boundaries. The volume lets readers hear the third president explain his decisions in formal, public language. It serves as a primary source for the politics and diplomacy of the early republic.
10894-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation of presidential messages and papers gives John Adams his own section, covering March 4, 1797, to March 4, 1801. A short life opens it: Adams was born near Boston in 1735, entered Harvard in 1751, studied law, taught at Worcester, and married Abigail Smith in 1764. He rose at the Boston bar before the Revolution.

The volume then prints Adams's messages, addresses, and proclamations as president, in official form. Richardson's series aimed to put every president's public papers within reach. Readers and researchers get Adams in his own words, with a compact life to set them in context.
10895-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James Madison takes centre stage in this volume of Richardson's presidential papers, covering March 1809 to March 1817. A sketch traces Madison from Virginia boyhood and Princeton through the Continental Congress and the 1787 Constitutional Convention, where he played a leading part. Service in the House and as Jefferson's Secretary of State preceded his own two terms.

Madison's messages then speak for themselves, including his war messages against Britain and his complaints about British commanders using Native allies in battle. Trade, finance, and the defence of the young republic run through the papers. Readers can follow a president guiding the nation through the War of 1812 and into peace, in documents written for Congress and the public.
10919-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's second volume of his compilation of presidential messages and papers, dated 1897, followed a first volume welcomed by Congress and the press. Congress ordered fifteen thousand additional copies of the whole publication after the first volume appeared about May 1, 1896. This volume adds a steel engraving of the Treasury building, with more public buildings to follow.

The work prints annual, special, and veto messages, inaugural addresses, proclamations, and other papers from the chief magistrate. Richardson's aim was a complete, official record for citizens and scholars. Readers get a stately source book of the early presidency, in its original form.
10951-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Volume five, part one, of James D. Richardson's compilation covers twelve years before the Civil War, from the Taylor-Fillmore administration through Pierce and Buchanan to March 1861. Richardson's preface names the great issues of the period: the Compromise of 1850, the admission of California, Minnesota, Oregon, and Kansas, the Gadsden Purchase, Kansas-Nebraska, the Dred Scott decision.

Veto messages feature strongly, as Pierce rejects land grants and internal improvements and Buchanan rejects homestead and agricultural bills. Buchanan's protests against a House inquiry into his conduct also appear. The volume is a primary source for the sectional crisis, showing presidents defending their policies in public while the Union slid toward war.
11021-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James Buchanan's presidency fills this volume of Richardson's compilation, covering March 1857 to March 1861. A sketch traces Buchanan from Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, where he was born in 1791 to a Scotch-Irish farmer, through Dickinson College and Lancaster law practice, to the state legislature, ten years in Congress.

Buchanan's papers then record the sectional crisis: Kansas, slavery, secession, and the defence of the Union as states left after Lincoln's election. Orders for half-hour guns and flags at half-staff after a statesman's death show the formal side of the office. The volume is a primary source for the last months of peace, written in the language of a president trying to hold a breaking nation together.
11034-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Martin Van Buren's presidency fills this volume of James D. Richardson's compilation, covering March 1837 to March 1841. A sketch traces Van Buren from Kinderhook, New York, where he was born in 1782, through law study at fourteen, the New York bar, and state politics as a Jeffersonian.

Van Buren's papers follow, including messages on Indian treaties, naval surveys, and lighthouse sites, sent to the Senate and to Speaker James K. Polk. The documents show a president managing finance, expansion, and federal administration after the Panic of 1837. Readers get the administration in its official voice, useful for studying Jacksonian politics and the presidency between Jackson and Tyler.
11125-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled this volume of the messages and papers of the presidents, covering Franklin Pierce, March 4, 1853, to March 4, 1857. Pierce was born in Hillsboro, New Hampshire, on November 23, 1804, fourth son of Benjamin Pierce, a Revolutionary soldier who became governor of New Hampshire. Franklin studied at Hancock, Francestown, and Exeter, then at Bowdoin College, where his mates included Longfellow and Hawthorne.

Pierce graduated in 1824, studied law, served in the New Hampshire legislature as speaker, then in Congress, where his first important speech urged economy and watchfulness against fraud. Later pages discuss claims against the government, noting that no president had deemed them worthy of recommendation to Congress. The volume preserves Pierce's messages and papers as a reference for historians of the 1850s.
1119-king-henry-v:
Henry V, the wild prince turned king, claims France, crosses the Channel, and wins the impossible victory of Agincourt against a far larger French army. William Shakespeare's history play follows him from the London taverns of his youth to the muddy field, with the Chorus begging the audience to imagine the rest.

Henry woos the French princess, rallies his men with the St. Crispin's Day speech, and proves a king of wit, nerve, and ruthlessness. The play's patriotism and its doubts sit side by side. It remains the great English war play, rousing and troubling at once.
11202-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's third volume of presidential papers, published by authority of Congress with copyright 1897, covers Andrew Jackson's second term and Martin Van Buren's presidency. It prints Jackson's reasons for removing deposits from the United States Bank, his Farewell Address. Papers on the gold-silver ratio, alongside Van Buren's message urging an independent treasury, the divorce of bank and state.

A dispute with Britain over the northeastern boundary also appears among Van Buren's papers. Richardson's preface notes the surprise that eight years could fill a volume, but argues the material matches earlier volumes in interest. For researchers, the book is a primary source for Jacksonian finance and diplomacy.
11230-macmillan-s-reading-books-book-v:
Macmillan's Reading Book V, for Standard V under the English and Scotch education codes, provided graded prose and poetry for schoolchildren facing state inspection. Pupils were expected to read with expression, recite at least seventy-five lines of poetry, and parse simple sentences, with three hundred lines required for the Scotch code's second-year literature subject. A preface explains the series as a systematic course matched to each standard.

The selections mix old ballads with standard authors, chosen so teachers could test meaning, allusion, and derivation. The book's interest now is educational: it shows what Victorian and Edwardian schools counted as literacy. Its apparatus of codes and grants reveals a classroom governed by examination.
11239-the-life-and-adventures-of-robinso:
This 1812 London edition prints Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe in two volumes, preceded by a life of Defoe tracing him from a London butcher's son to pamphleteer and author. Crusoe's own narrative follows: shipwreck, solitude on an island, and slow mastery of farming, building, and survival over many years. Friday's arrival later turns the solitary tale into a story of companionship and rule.

The edition matters because it shows Crusoe as early nineteenth-century readers met him, framed as a true account written by himself. Its long life testifies to the book's grip on ideas of self-reliance and empire. Modern readers can follow both the adventure and the period attitudes embedded in it.
11314-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's first volume of presidential papers, issued in 1897 under the Joint Committee on Printing, opens the series with a preface defending the project. presidential messages, vetoes, orders, and addresses are among the most valuable parts of American public writing. Richardson gathered nearly all proclamations, addresses, messages, and letters to Congress, leaving out only nominations, treaty notes, and department reports.

The volume sets the pattern for the series, making founding-era papers handy in compact form for lawmakers, students, and scholars. Its claim is practical: no earlier government publication had collected these papers together. Readers still use Richardson's book as a gateway to early presidential writing.
12318-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled this eighth volume of presidential messages and papers in 1897, covering March 4, 1881, to March 4, 1889. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, gathered official documents for Congress and the public.

The volume spans the Garfield-Arthur term and Cleveland first term. It opens with Garfield assassination: the president shot at a station and carried to a private room. He was later removed to the Executive Mansion, while Vice President Arthur succeeded him, the fourth such succession in American history. Later papers cover tariffs, civil service, and foreign affairs. The book is a reference work, valuable for the documents themselves rather than for narrative.
12462-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's sixth volume of presidential papers covers March 1861 to March 1869, the administrations of Lincoln and Johnson. Richardson notes that no period since the Revolution holds so many events of surpassing importance. Lincoln's years were given to civil war, Johnson's to restoring peace and the Union as it had stood.

Messages, proclamations and state papers follow in order, letting readers trace war, emancipation, reconstruction and impeachment in official words. Richardson calls Lincoln a kind-hearted humanitarian who loved peace, yet had to wage a bloody conflict. The volume is a primary source for the Civil War era, valuable precisely because it lets documents speak before historians summarise them.
12463-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation gathers the messages and papers of James K. Polk, president from March 1845 to March 1849. A short life opens the volume, tracing Polk from his birth in North Carolina in 1795, through a Tennessee farm boyhood, to the White House, before the documents themselves begin.

Inside are presidential messages to Congress, proclamations and state papers of an administration that annexed Texas, settled Oregon and fought Mexico. Read in sequence they show how Polk stated his aims, defended his acts and managed a fast-expanding nation. The volume serves as a primary source, letting readers hear a presidency in its own official voice rather than through later summary.
12464-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's volume on John Tyler covers April 1841 to March 1845, opening with Tyler's life. Born at Greenway, Virginia, in 1790, son of a governor, Tyler graduated from William and Mary in 1807, loved history and music, played the violin, and entered the bar in 1809. Election to the legislature followed in 1811.

As president after Harrison's death, Tyler faced annexation, tariff and party quarrels, and his messages and papers record those struggles in official form. Richardson's compilation lets readers follow a much-criticised presidency through its own documents. The volume serves students of the 1840s, when Texas, Oregon and party division shaped the road to later crisis.
12754-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's volume on Chester A. Arthur covers September 1881 to March 1885, opening with Arthur's life. Born in Fairfield, Vermont, on 5 October 1830, Arthur was eldest son of Reverend William Arthur, a Baptist minister born in Ireland, and Malvina Stone. He prepared at Union Village and Schenectady, entering Union College as a sophomore in 1845.

Teaching terms at Schaghticoke and Psi Upsilon membership follow. He was elected as one of six in a class of one hundred to Phi Beta Kappa, for high scholarship. As president after Garfield's death, Arthur faced civil service reform, tariffs and party strife, recorded in messages and papers. The volume offers a primary source for a quiet, surprising presidency.
12755-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Compiled by James D. Richardson, this volume gathers the public papers of President Andrew Johnson, from April 1865 to March 1869. A short life opens the book. Johnson was born poor in Raleigh in 1808, apprenticed to a tailor at ten, taught the alphabet by a fellow worker, and helped to write by his wife Eliza. Office by office, Johnson rose from alderman to president.

The bulk is official text: messages to Senate and House, reports, vetoes, and notes on treaties, including a Hawaiian reciprocity treaty in 1867. Readers get Johnson's Reconstruction years in his own formal voice. The volume serves historians who need the primary record, not a retelling.
13012-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's seventh volume of presidential papers covers Ulysses S. Grant's eight years and Rutherford B. Hayes's four, from March 1869 to March 1881. The prefatory note calls Grant's election a republic's gratitude to a successful soldier, who would never have risen without the Civil War. Restoration of southern states and reunion of the Union mark the period.

Grant's messages press civil service reform, asking Congress for strength to carry out a commission's rules, set to take effect on January 1, 1872. The volume gives the primary record of Reconstruction's close. Historians will find here Grant and Hayes in their own formal words.
13021-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation gathers the official papers of President Rutherford B. Hayes, who served from March 4, 1877, to March 4, 1881. A short life opens the volume: Hayes was born in Delaware, Ohio, in 1822, studied Latin and Greek, entered Kenyon College in 1838, and won praise as a debater. The main text then gives his messages to Congress in full.

Hayes writes on yellow fever and the need for national sanitary control, sending tents and rations worth about twenty-five thousand dollars to stricken towns. He returns again and again to the franchise, urging full and safe voting for all citizens. The volume is a primary source for Reconstruction's end, in the president's own formal words.
13235-in-the-ranks-of-the-c-i-v:
Driver Erskine Childers, a clerk in the House of Commons, published In the Ranks of the C.I.V. in 1900 as a diary of service with the City Imperial Volunteers battery in South Africa. Childers dedicates it to his friend and comrade Gunner Basil Williams. Chapters run from the Montfort and Cape Town through Bloemfontein, Lindley, Bethlehem, and on to Pretoria.

Childers records stable duty, icy washes from an ammunition box, frost at night, and snug lairs under quartermaster's stores. Shifting camp a mile brings grumbles, as fuel and meal must be decanted into tins and wallets. The diary is a vivid, unheroic record of volunteer war: marching, waiting, and small comforts kept with care.
13617-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiles the messages and papers of the presidents in volume nine, published by authority of Congress in 1902, covering Benjamin Harrison and Grover Cleveland's second term to March 4, 1897. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, began the work in April 1895 after the Fifty-third Congress and gave it his whole time outside official duties.

Sugar beet cultivation, civil service law, and the transfer of sugar supervision to the Department of Agriculture fill Harrison and Cleveland papers. Greer County, occupied by Texas citizens on more than a million and a half acres, is claimed by Choctaws and Chickasaws, with the United States suing to declare it Indian country. The volume is a documentary record of two administrations.
14137-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
This volume gathers the public papers of Grover Cleveland's second term, from March 1893 to March 1897. Inaugural and annual messages lead, with Cleveland pledging devotion to the people's welfare and warning against tendencies that menace sound government. Vetoes, proclamations, and messages to Congress follow in order, forming a record of a presidency rather than a narrative life.

Foreign and domestic business fills the pages. Cleveland sends condolences on President Carnot's death, protests a revived German ban on American cattle over Texas fever, and disputes a sugar duty aimed at bounty-paying countries. At home he reports on Armenian-born naturalized citizens in Turkey and urges payment for rail transport of colonists returned from Mexico to Alabama. Historians value the set as a primary source, dense but exact.
14417-the-agamemnon-of-aeschylus-transla:
Gilbert Murray, Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford, rendered Aeschylus's Agamemnon into English rhyming verse, with explanatory notes, in this popular edition. The play, first performed in Athens in 458 BC, opens the Oresteia trilogy.

A watchman waits for the beacon announcing Troy's fall, and King Agamemnon returns home to his wife Clytemnestra, his captive prophetess Cassandra, and a murderous welcome. The chorus of Argive elders meditates on pride, guilt, and fate. Murray's verse keeps the drama singable, and his notes guide readers through the Greek stagecraft. Later translations owe much to his clear, musical line.
1521-king-henry-v:
Shakespeare's Henry V follows the former Prince Hal, now king, from a London council chamber to the fields of Agincourt. A chorus begs the audience to imagine great armies with few players, and the play moves from Harfleur's siege to the eve of battle, where Henry walks disguised among his men.

The St Crispin's Day speech and the victory over a larger French force crown a king who has learned both war and mercy. The play is Shakespeare's most stirring history. It celebrates leadership while letting the costs of war, in camp and court, show through the glory.
15863-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
A volume from the great compilation of presidential messages and papers, in the Richardson tradition. The volume opens with Grover Cleveland and his first term, March 1885 to March 1889. A short life of Cleveland fronts the papers, tracing his family from Moses Cleveland of Ipswich to his father, a Yale minister. Official texts follow in full.

Messages to Congress, proclamations, and executive orders show Cleveland at work: vetoes, civil service, and the tariff fight. The compilation's value lies in completeness, letting readers hear a president in his own words. For students of the Gilded Age, the volume gives the record straight, without later comment to soften it.
16415-tales-from-many-sources-vol-v:
This 1886 volume gathers seven tales first printed in magazines like Temple Bar and Belgravia. Juliana H. Ewing opens with Lob Lie-by-the-Fire, about a rough house elf who threshes corn by night for a bowl of cream. A balloon trip, a tale of Virginia, a numbered prisoner, and a Goneril story follow.

The mix is wide: folk fancy, modern life, and quiet social drama sit side by side. Each tale can be read alone, and the range shows what magazine fiction offered late Victorian readers. The Ewing opener is the gem, full of north-country charm, but the whole set rewards a reader who likes short stories with varied moods.
17845-salem-witchcraft-volumes-i-and-ii-:
Charles W. Upham wrote Salem Witchcraft, first printed in 1867 and reissued by Frederick Ungar in New York, joining volumes one and two in a single text. Upham, a Salem man and scholar, set out to give both the village story and a history of views on witchcraft.

Volume one covers Salem Village and the rise of witch belief, while volume two follows the trials at Salem Village itself, with a supplement and appendix. Maps, lists, and a general index aid the reader. Upham writes with care and moral force, and his work still stands as a classic, humane study of the 1692 delusion.
18524-a-dark-month-from-swinburne-s-coll:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's A Dark Month appears here as taken from volume five of his collected poetical works, published by William Heinemann in London in 1917. Volume five gathers Studies in Song, A Century of Roundels, Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets, and the Heptalogia, with other pieces. A Dark Month stands among the shorter poems of that set, first printed by Chatto in 1904.

The poem takes Victor Hugo's line as epigraph: la maison sans enfants, the house without children. That phrase sets the month's darkness: a house, a loss, and a season of grief. Swinburne writes in his musical, elegiac manner, with the sea and the year turning behind the personal sorrow. Readers get a short, somber lyric from a poet known for fire: a dark month, a childless house, and verse that holds grief in form.
20762-chancellorsville-and-gettysburg-ca:
Abner Doubleday fought at Gettysburg, and his campaign history speaks with a soldier's frankness. He warns that fresh events draw sharp fire from those who lived them. A bland tale that praises all and blames none, he says, would waste the war's hard lessons.

Chancellorsville and Gettysburg, two vast battles of 1863, fill this volume of the Campaigns of the Civil War set. Doubleday held ground at Gettysburg on the first day. His account weighs plans, ground, and command choices in plain terms. Readers get a Union view from a man who stood in the line himself.
2253-king-henry-v:
Henry V, once the wild Prince Hal, claims the French throne and leads a small English army to Agincourt. Shakespeare's history follows the king from the tennis-ball insult through the siege of Harfleur to the St Crispin's Day speech. The Chorus begs the audience to imagine vast battles on a bare stage. The victory comes at terrible cost.

Around the heroics, the play questions war itself: soldiers debate the king's responsibility the night before battle, and Falstaff's old friends die in its shadow. Henry's wooing of Katherine closes the action with humor and hope. It is both a patriotic pageant and a study of leadership.
22796-impressions-of-america-during-the-:
Tyrone Power wrote Impressions of America during the Years 1833, 1834, and 1835, a celebrated Irish actor's account of his American tours. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Power, grandfather of the later stage and film stars of his name, played to packed houses from New York to New Orleans and wrote down what he saw.

His aim, stated in the preface, is repayment. If he can dissipate one common error, he says, he will be content. Eradicating one vulgar prejudice, or kindling one kindly feeling, would do as well. Then he would have returned the high favor with which America repaid his efforts to please. The volumes that follow mix theater gossip with sharp notes on manners, politics, and slavery. Power's America is the young republic seen by a friendly, watchful guest.
23284-impressions-of-america-during-the-:
Impressions of America records a traveller's view of the United States in the years 1833, 1834, and 1835. Not every impression is of crowds or politics. One passage sits in the upper gallery of a house upon a cliff, watching the rising moon at work.

Moonlight throws a golden bridge across the water, from the far horizon to the beach below. Such a sight, the writer says, would be worth something in a poet's or painter's eyes. Readers get an early foreign account of America that mixes close observation of a young republic with outright wonder at its scenery.
24195-history-of-the-159th-regiment-n-y-:
This history of the 159th Regiment, New York State Volunteers, was compiled from the diary of Lieutenant Edward Duffy. It was published in New York in 1890, reprinted from the Hudson Gazette of 1865 in one hundred and fifty copies. In late October 1862, the 167th Regiment under Colonel Homer A. Nelson at Hudson joined with the 159th under Lieutenant-Colonel Edward L. Molineux at Brooklyn, keeping the 159th name with Nelson in command.

The regiment left Camp Kelly at Hudson on October 30 and sailed on the steamer Connecticut. It marched to Park Barracks in New York, and was mustered into United States service on November 1 by Lieutenant R. B. Smith. From Castle Garden it went by steamboat to Staten Island and Camp New Dorp. Readers get a Civil War regiment's record, kept close to a diary.
28050-women-as-sex-vendors-or-why-women-:
R. B. Tobias and Mary E. Marcy published Women as Sex Vendors, or Why Women Are Conservative, in Chicago with Charles H. Kerr and Company in 1918, subtitled a view of the economic status of woman. The book argues that women, as owners of a commodity vital to men's health and well-being, occupy a favored biologic and economic position.

Because the favored class rarely revolts against a system that advantages it, women have seldom been revolutionists, while a true revolutionist owns nothing to sell except his power to work. The socialist-feminist argument, blunt in its title, remains a provocative early statement on sex, economics, and conservatism.
29854-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-v:
Volume five of the works of Aphra Behn gathers her short fiction, with notes placed after each story in this text. The Epistle Dedicatory to Oroonoko, printed as an appendix in the book, stands just before the novel itself, as the editor intended. Cross-references from other volumes of the complete works follow the notes, and the New English Dictionary is now known as the Oxford English Dictionary.

Thirteen tales fill the volume, from The Adventure of the Black Lady and The Court of the King of Bantam to The Fair Jilt and The Unfortunate Happy Lady. Oroonoko, or The Royal Slave, stands at the heart of the set, with Agnes de Castro and The History of the Nun beside it. The Lucky Mistake, The Dumb Virgin, and The Wandering Beauty close the run. The book is a rich shelf of Restoration prose fiction.
29878-the-history-of-woman-suffrage-volu:
Ida Husted Harper edited volume five of The History of Woman Suffrage, covering 1900 to 1920, printed in 1922 for the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Its motto reads After Seventy Years Came the Victory. A frontispiece shows Dr. Anna Howard Shaw, vice-president-at-large of the association from 1892 to 1904 and president from 1904 to 1915. Copperplate and photogravure engravings illustrate the volume, the fifth of six.

Chapter one treats the founding of the National Association and its work for a federal amendment, state amendments, and other reforms. The annual convention at Minneapolis in 1901 and Mrs. Stanton's address on the church, the Bible, and woman suffrage follow. The volume carries the movement from the turn of the century to the vote itself, written by the women who led it, with documents close at hand.
31156-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume six, slice one of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the alphabet from Châtelet to Chicago. Its article list runs from Chatham, Chatsworth, and Chattanooga through Chatterji, Bankim Chandra, Chatterton, Chaucer, and the Cherokee. It goes on to chess, chemistry, and the cheetah, with entries on places, people, arts, and sciences in between.

As a slice of the great 1910 reference work, the volume shows the Britannica's method at full stretch: concise, authoritative articles meant to answer a reader's question in a few pages. For modern users, it doubles as a snapshot of what the Edwardian world thought worth knowing, from French towns to American cities.
31771-si-klegg-book-1-his-transformation:
John McElroy's first Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1910, follows Si's transformation from a raw recruit to a veteran. Its twenty-two chapters run from going to war and Si's complete equipment through the deadly bayonet, the old canteen, and the awful hardtack. Fat pork is described as indispensable body timber for patriotism.

Si is detailed as cook, joins the awkward squad, gets a letter, meets the doctors, straggles, handles mules, and at last comes under fire, fights, and captures a prisoner. Readers get the opening volume of a beloved Civil War comedy, built from sketches first published in The National Tribune.
32604-the-story-of-the-raising-and-organ:
Ellis Spear, a brevet brigadier general, tells how a volunteer regiment was raised and put in the field in 1862. Read before the Military Order of the Loyal Legion in 1903, his paper skips battles. Instead it explains the unglamorous start of soldiering.

Private men recruited at their own cost under the governor's writ, hoping for commissions in the companies they raised. Spear follows them into camp, where drill at first looks like a town meeting. He shows how raw men and green officers slowly learned to march, dress ranks, and parade.
35092-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, volume eight holds heads from Ehud to Electroscope. This hosted text is that one bound book of the great set in full. Signs in the text stand for math marks that plain type can not show. Notes list print slips found and set right in two of its heads.

Town lore on a Ukraine mill town stands among the heads in this stretch. A long head on the spring of stuff treats how frames bend and spring back. Glass and hard stone are said to show near no true give at all. Brass, steel, and white gold rank high in the spring class of stuff. The set was the peak of the age for facts in one shelf work.
36104-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, is represented here by the slice of a volume running alphabetically from Fox, George to France. The eleventh edition of 1910 to 1911 was the most famous the encyclopaedia ever made, and its volumes were broken into letter ranges for the modern reprint. The index matter at the head of the text shows the run of entries in this stretch.

Within a few pages the alphabet carries the reader from the Fox family and Foxe, the martyrologist, to foxglove the plant, Framingham and Framlingham the towns, and Franc the coin. George Fox the Quaker founder and Charles James Fox the statesman anchor the long Fox sequence. The slice is reference matter in its purest form: signed articles, cross-references and bibliographies, compressed into the dense double columns that made the eleventh edition the scholar's Britannica.
36387-colonial-expeditions-to-the-interi:
Cook gathers the colonial expeditions into California's Central Valley in this anthropology paper. It appeared as volume sixteen, number six of the Anthropological Records at Berkeley in 1960. The price of $1.50 stands on the title page of the university publication.

Early expeditions from 1776 to 1803 open the contents at page 241. Excerpts from official correspondence and Sal's expedition of 1796 fill that section in the list. Spanish soldiers and missionaries rode into the valley after Indians and runaways, and Cook prints their reports to show a lost world of tule marshes and great herds of people.
36548-a-plain-introduction-to-the-critic:
Frederick Henry Ambrose Scrivener wrote this plain guide to the criticism of the New Testament for biblical students. George Bell and Sons published the fourth edition at London in 1894, with Edward Miller as editor. Miller had been a fellow and tutor at New College, Oxford, and Scrivener was by then dead.

First come the general character of the copies, the divisions of the text, and the large uncial manuscripts. Then come the cursive copies of the Gospels, the Acts, the Catholic Epistles, the letters of Paul, and the Apocalypse. The last chapters cover the service books of the Gospels, while the appendices treat facsimiles and dating by indiction. Scrivener had collated more manuscripts than any English scholar of his age, and his guide trained students for generations.
36549-a-plain-introduction-to-the-critic:
A Plain Introduction to the Criticism of the New Testament, volume two, reached a fourth edition in 1894. The author, Frederick Henry Ambrose Scrivener, had died before it appeared. Edward Miller, once a fellow of New College, Oxford, edited the new issue for George Bell and Sons. Scrivener's fresh notes on sacred Greek manuscripts are worked into it.

The volume treats the tools that stand behind the Greek text. Chapters cover the ancient versions: Syriac, Latin, Egyptian and others. Citations by the early church writers come next, then printed and critical editions. Internal evidence and the history of the text follow. Select passages are tested at the end, with indexes of texts and subjects to guide the student.
37198-the-deluge-an-historical-novel-of-:
Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote The Deluge, an historical novel of Poland, Sweden, and Russia, here in the first of two volumes. Jeremiah Curtin made the authorized, unabridged translation from the Polish. Little, Brown and Company published this library edition at Boston in 1915; Curtin's copyright dates to 1891. The Deluge stands as sequel to With Fire and Sword. A list of Sienkiewicz's works in Curtin's versions stands at the front.

Curtin dedicates his translation to Charles A Dana, editor of the New York Sun. Dana, he writes, knows great events from personal contact, not books merely. He takes pleasure in many literatures and in the points that distinguish nations. The Deluge will turn his attention to a new field of history, Curtin hopes. The novel treats the Swedish invasion that nearly drowned the Polish commonwealth in the 1650s.
37308-the-deluge-an-historical-novel-of-:
Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote The Deluge, a war novel of Poland, Sweden, and Russia, Englished by Jeremiah Curtin. Little, Brown, and Company issued volume two in Boston in nineteen hundred fifteen. Curtin held rights to his text from eighteen hundred ninety one. The book stands as a sequel to With Fire and Sword.

Swedish guns pound the shrine fort of Yasna Gora in this part. Its monks stall for time with smooth talk and terms. General Miller sends Colonel Kuklinovski in with fresh threats. The prior shows that the king’s writ names a town, not the shrine. Night truce lets both sides dig and mend. No man fell in the first storm of shot, the monks marvel. Faith and craft hold the walls as winter nears.
37523-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Geoponici to Germany. It is one of the set's alphabetical volumes, gathering hundreds of signed articles. Among its longest entries are Georgia, German Literature, and Germany itself.

Shorter entries include George the Third and George the Syncellus, a patriarch's confidential companion. The Georgia article treats the American state's legislature and the governor's veto. It notes that a two-thirds vote may override a veto, even on single items of appropriation bills. The Germany article describes the Elbe sandstone range and the Lusatian hills. East of the Elbe, it says, coniferous trees prevail, especially the Scotch fir. A transcriber's note records corrected misprints and explains the volume's subscripts, superscripts, and Greek letters.
39627-english-and-scottish-ballads-volum:
Child's great collection of English and Scottish ballads reaches volume five in this copy. Archaic and dialect spellings are retained as printed, the transcriber's notes explain at the front. Footnotes are numbered in sequence through the book and placed for the reader's use in the text.

Child gathered ballads from manuscripts and old prints, with variants compared in his notes. Murder ballads, border raids, love songs and supernatural tales fill such a volume in his ordering. The set remains a standard storehouse for folk singers and scholars, drawn from the singing and printing of centuries in England and Scotland.
39773-juvenile-styles-original-designs-f:
Juvenile Styles is a pattern book of knitted and crocheted clothes for babies and children, designed by Mary Hoyer. The hosted copy is volume four, number seven, printed in Reading, Pennsylvania. Hoyer copyrighted the designs in 1941, and the book speaks to mothers knitting for the 1946-47 season.

Each design gives needles, yarn amounts, and gauge before the row-by-row steps. An early pattern makes a matching jacket set for a mother and her three-month-old baby. Hoyer promises that beginners and experts alike can follow with confidence. The book also sells its own style books by mail for thirty cents. It shows home knitting as both craft and care for family.
40556-the-lord-s-coming-miscellaneous-wr:
This second volume of the Miscellaneous Writings of Mackintosh gathers his shorter papers on Bible subjects. Loizeaux Brothers of New York first issued the collection in 1898. The title piece is a long set of papers on the Lord's coming, the hope of Christ's return. It runs to more than a hundred pages.

Other papers treat Abraham and Lot under the title The Call of God. Thou and Thy House speaks to the Christian at home. Further pieces cover discipleship in an evil day, sin in the flesh and on the conscience, the unequal yoke, and Gideon and his companions. Poems and short pieces on eternal punishment fill out the volume. Mackintosh wrote for the Plymouth Brethren, and his notes on Romans and Genesis were widely read.
40769-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One slice of the fifteenth volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from the article on Edward Kelly to the article on Kite. The eleventh edition was the great modern form of the Britannica, a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. This slice carries biographies of the Kellys and the Kembles, the actor family, and long articles on Lord Kelvin and on Kierkegaard.

Place articles crowd the alphabet: Kelso, Kendal, Kenilworth, Kiel, Kiev, Kilkenny, and Kilimanjaro among them. Captain Kidd gets his article under his three namesakes, John, Thomas, and William Kidd, and subjects run from kelp and kidnapping to kidney diseases. The slice is a cross-section of the edition's method: scholarship alphabetized, one column of the world's knowledge at a time.
41902-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Hosted text here is one volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, covering entries from L to Lamellibranchia. A long transcriber's note stands at the front. It explains how subscripts, superscripts, and side notes were handled in the copy. Greek letters and the root symbol are marked by set signs, the note says. Side notes were moved to serve as titles of their paragraphs.

The note also lists printers' errors that were corrected. Among them are slips in the articles on lace, Laconia, and La Farge. A table in the text sets out the earlier editions of the work. The fifth edition ran to twenty volumes in eighteen fifteen to seventeen, the note's table shows. The entries in this volume run from labyrinth terms to a group of molluscs.
42693-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-x:
Number twenty-six of Harper's New Monthly Magazine is dated July 1852, in the monthly's fifth volume. The magazine mixed tales, travel, and fact pieces for the American home.

Jacob Abbott leads with The Armory at Springfield. He opens on the Connecticut River as it winds through Massachusetts. Broad meadows, enriched by yearly floods, spread for miles on each bank. Villages rise on high ground, safe from the water. Greenfield, Northampton, and Springfield stand as the three chief towns of the valley. Abbott paints the scene before he enters the armory town itself. One number like this shows the young magazine's rich, calm style.
43043-george-eliot-s-life-as-related-in-:
J W Cross arranged and edited George Eliot's Life, as told in her letters and journals, in three volumes. Cross was the novelist's husband, and this first volume is called Unknown. Harper and Brothers issued the set at New York, with pictures.

Cross let the life write itself, as far as he could, from her own words. He held that this plan best shows the growth of her mind and character. Other voices appear only in marked blocks of quoted matter. A combined index for all three volumes stands at the end of the third. The works list names Adam Bede and Middlemarch.
43044-george-eliot-s-life-as-related-in-:
George Eliot Life, volume two, retells her life through letters and journals. Her husband Cross arranged and edited the three volume set. This second volume is titled Famous in the set plan. Harper and Brothers of New York issued the library edition.

A transcriber note explains how Cross text and quoted text are set apart. Passages from other writers appear in block quotes through the volume. A portrait of Eliot, engraved by Stodart, fronts the volume here. The publisher list names her works, from Adam Bede to Daniel Deronda. Readers trace the famed years of a major novelist through her own words.
43045-george-eliot-s-life-as-related-in-:
George Eliot's Life as Related in Her Letters and Journals, Volume Three, is the final volume of the biography arranged and edited by her husband Cross. It was printed at New York by Harper and Brothers. The volume's name in the set is Sunset, and its motto runs: our finest hope is finest memory. An illustration shows Number 4 Cheyne Walk, Chelsea, her last London house.

A tour in Spain opens the volume, and The Spanish Gypsy follows. The years 1869 to 1872 hold the poems and Middlemarch. Then come Daniel Deronda, and the illness and death of George Henry Lewes in 1878. The last chapter covers Theophrastus Such, her marriage with Cross, and the end. A combined index to the whole set stands at the back.
43368-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-x:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine offered this number for August 1852, volume five, number twenty-seven. The lead piece is Jacob Abbott's Memoirs of the Holy Land, opening with a view of Mount Carmel from the sea.

Abbott pictures the traveler on deck at dawn, called up to see the sacred shore. Mount Carmel rises bold above the coast, crowned by an old convent. A map shows the provinces of Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. Abbott explains how the Carmel range runs from the central hills down to the sea. His memoirs gave American readers a guided tour of Bible lands. The magazine mixed such travel writing with stories, poems, and news of books.
46424-cyclopedia-of-commerce-accountancy:
The Cyclopedia of Commerce, Accountancy, and Business Administration is a ten-volume set from the American Technical Society in Chicago, and volume 1 came out in 1910 with copyrights from 1909. A corps of auditors, accountants, attorneys, and specialists made the set, which holds over two thousand engravings and runs to ten volumes. A view of the mailing department of the Western Electric Company fronts this volume, and James Bray Griffith of the American School of Correspondence was managing editor.

Robert H Montgomery of Lybrand, Ross Bros and Montgomery edited Dicksee's Auditing for America. Arthur Lowes Dickinson of Price, Waterhouse and his own firm, William M Lybrand, and F H Macpherson added more weight. The subtitle lists the scope: accounting, auditing, bookkeeping, and commercial law, with banking, advertising, selling, cost keeping, and systematising.
46448-cyclopedia-of-commerce-accountancy:
Volume two of the Cyclopedia of Commerce, Accountancy, and Business Administration came out in Chicago in 1910. The work runs to ten volumes and more than two thousand engravings. A bird's-eye view of the Baldwin Locomotive Works at Philadelphia shows the scale of the industry it serves.

A corps of auditors, accountants, attorneys, and specialists in business methods prepared the set. It covers accounting, auditing, bookkeeping, and commercial law, then banking, advertising, selling, and cost keeping. Office and factory records and the systematizing of work get full treatment. Montgomery, a noted accountant, stands among the collaborators. The set was a whole business school in books, sold to clerks and managers who studied at home.
46489-cyclopedia-of-commerce-accountancy:
Cyclopedia of Commerce, Accountancy and Business Administration, volume three, is part of a ten-volume reference work issued at Chicago in 1910 by the American Technical Society. A corps of auditors, accountants, attorneys and business specialists prepared the set for the working clerk and manager. Its pages cover accounting, auditing and bookkeeping, and they also treat banking, advertising, selling and cost keeping, with over two thousand engravings.

The front matter names the men who did the work. It names Robert Montgomery of Lybrand, Ross Brothers and Montgomery and Arthur Dickinson of Price Waterhouse. It also names the author of a work on loose-leaf bookkeeping and a systems man from the Burroughs Adding Machine firm. The managing editor led the commerce department of the American School of Correspondence, which held the copyright.
46545-cyclopedia-of-commerce-accountancy:
Cyclopedia of Commerce, Accountancy, Business Administration, volume four, came from the American Technical Society at Chicago in 1910, under a 1909 copyright held by the American School of Correspondence. The full set runs to ten volumes, and the books hold more than two thousand engravings in all.

Volume four deals with the day to day work of trade, with parts on banking, selling, cost keeping, bookkeeping, and the records of an office or a factory. A large team made the books: men who checked the accounts of firms, men of law, and men who knew how shops and offices should be run. James Bray Griffith, who led the school's commerce work, was the managing editor in charge of the whole set. The team also had Robert Montgomery, of a great accountancy firm, who edited the American edition of Dicksee's Auditing.
47091-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
The Church published this first volume of its history at Salt Lake City in 1902. Deseret News printed it. B H Roberts supplied the introduction and notes.

Period one gives the history of Joseph Smith, the Prophet, by himself. The preface calls the task a solemn duty to the Saints and to the world. The events of the Church's rise, it says, are the most weighty that history can record. Eyewitness words give the best proof, so Smith's own manuscript history forms the body. The editors admit the cost: the work reads more as annals than as shaped history. Events may end far from where they began.
47192-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, volume two, tells Joseph Smith’s tale. Smith wrote the history in his own person, as its title owns. B H Roberts shaped the book with front talks and full notes. The Church issued it at Salt Lake City in nineteen hundred four.

Zion’s Camp marches at the front of Roberts’s wide survey here. The first school movement and the foreign mission plan share that talk. Keys for the gathering of Israel and Elijah’s mission crown it. Chapter one takes up the year eighteen hundred thirty four. Missouri wrongs and Kirtland mob threats darken its first pages. Wesley Hurlburt, cast out and tried, fills much of that year. The High Council’s founding and its first cases fill chapter two. Jackson County’s war on the Saints grounds chapter three’s grave tale.
47707-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
Volume three of the History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was printed in Salt Lake City in 1905. It covers the years when Joseph Smith and his followers moved into Missouri. Roberts supplied the opening essay and the notes that run through the book. The main text rests on Smith's own account of his life and work.

Roberts opens by asking why the Saints met such harsh treatment in Missouri. He weighs slavery, fear of their growing vote, and ties with the Indians, and finds fault on both sides. The chapters then follow the flight from Kirtland, the welcome at Far West, and church trials of old leaders. Oliver Cowdery and David Whitmer, once close to Smith, both face charges and lose their places.
48841-life-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-:
Life of Napoleon Bonaparte, volume five, is part of Sir Walter Scott's biography, in the pocket edition published by Black of Edinburgh in 1876. An illustration of Hougoumont faces the contents, though the volume treats 1814. Chapter seventy-five follows Buonaparte marching upon Blucher, who holds Soissons. He attacks the place without success, and the battles of Craonne and Laon follow.

Napoleon attacks Rheims, and his marshals are defeated at Bar-sur-Aube and forced to retreat toward Paris. Chapter seventy-six crosses the Marne on March 22 and brings Marmont and Mortier back under the walls of Paris. Maria Louisa leaves the city with the civil authorities, and Paris is attacked on the thirtieth; a truce is accorded, and Joseph flies. Chapter seventy-seven surveys the parties in Paris: royalists, revolutionists, and the feelings of the lowest and middling classes. A summary preserved in the copy reaches the end.
50812-the-story-of-my-struggles-the-memo:
The Story of My Struggles is the memoir of Arminius Vambéry, professor of Oriental languages at Budapest. Fisher Unwin printed the first volume in London in 1904. A frontispiece shows the professor at seventy. Vambéry had also written The Story of Hungary and a book of his life and adventures.

The chapters start with his antecedents and infancy, then his juvenile struggles. He becomes a private tutor, then sets out on a first journey to the East. A second journey follows, and a return to Europe. Vambéry opens by refusing a long account of his pedigree, since genealogy is not among his favourite subjects. What he promises instead is the tale of a poor Hungarian boy who fought his way to fame as a traveller and scholar of the East.
50837-the-story-of-my-struggles-the-memo:
Arminius Vambery wrote The Story of My Struggles, and volume two came out in London in nineteen hundred four. T Fisher Unwin issued the life story. Vambery taught eastern tongues at the University of Budapest. A photo from Tehran in eighteen hundred sixty three faces the title page.

Friends asked why he left fame in England to settle in Hungary. He says love of home and his birth shaped the choice. No firm offer of work came from London hosts, he adds. Later chapters cover his work in public life in England. He tells of time at the English court. Talks with Sultan Abdul Hamid fill one long chapter. His tale ends, in his phrase, with no true end.
51063-john-call-dalton-m-d-u-s-v:
John Call Dalton, a surgeon in the Union Army, left a narrative of his personal military experience, privately printed in 1892 by his family. Charles Dalton holds the copyright, and the Riverside Press at Cambridge printed the book. A note says the pages begin a narrative written during the last year of Dalton's life, at the request of his family.

The book was printed for the instruction of the younger generation of the family, in March 1892. Dalton was also a famed physiologist, the first full professor of that science in the United States. His war record joins field hospitals to a life of science. Readers get a quiet, private memoir, never meant for the market, and all the more honest for it.
51217-footprints-of-the-red-men-indian-g:
Footprints of the Red Men, by Ruttenber, studies Indian geographical names in the Hudson River valley, the Mohawk valley, and on the Delaware. The book was issued in 1906 under the New York State Historical Association. Ruttenber also wrote a history of the Indian tribes of Hudson's River. Maps show the Hudson and New Netherland.

A motto from Trumbull holds that Indian place names are not empty sounds but word pictures of each place. Ruttenber sets out to fix where old names belong, from official records, and to match them to the look of the land. He notes that some names were kept while their true spots were lost. The study serves local historians and lovers of the region's deep past.
51514-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
The Historians' History of the World runs to twenty-five volumes, and this text holds one of them. Henry Smith Williams edited the set, with the help of a board of advisers and contributors. A portrait of Rawlinson, the great student of the ancient East, stands among the front images.

The set bills itself as a full narrative of the rise and growth of nations, as recorded by over two thousand great writers of all ages. Instead of one voice, it stitches the best historians into one long story. Readers can follow empires from their dawn to their fall, in the words of classic authorities. The volume shows how Edwardian families bought world history by the shelf.
51551-the-russian-campaign-april-to-augu:
Stanley Washburn, special correspondent of The Times with the Russian armies, wrote this account of the Russian campaign from April to August 1915. Melrose printed it in London as the second volume of his Field Notes from the Russian Front. Mewes took the photographs on tour with him.

Chapters open with the fall of Przemyśl and Warsaw in April. Washburn visits the Rawka and Bzura lines and walks the trenches. He reports how the Russians met the first gas attack, with grim detail. The German drive through Galicia and the loss of Warsaw close the book. Washburn writes as an eyewitness who liked the Russian soldier. His notes give the Eastern Front a human face.
51676-cyclopedia-of-commerce-accountancy:
Cyclopedia of Commerce, Accountancy, Business Administration is a general reference work in ten volumes. The American Technical Society published it in Chicago in 1910. Copyright rested with the American School of Correspondence, which devised the set. A view of the Union Stock Yards fronts this volume as its emblem.

The title page lists the fields the work claims to cover between its boards. Accounting, auditing, bookkeeping, and commercial law stand first among them. Business management, banking, advertising, and selling follow in the same breath. Office and factory records, cost keeping, and systematizing complete the survey. More than two thousand engravings illustrate the ten volumes throughout. A corps of auditors, accountants, attorneys, and specialists prepared the text. James Bray Griffith served as managing editor of the whole enterprise.
52177-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Henry Smith Williams edited The Historians' History of the World, a narrative of the rise and development of nations in twenty-five volumes. The Outlook Company published the set in New York in 1905. Williams gathered passages from more than two thousand great writers of all ages. A board of advisers from Berlin, Oxford, Paris, Vienna, and Harvard helped him shape the work.

This file holds volume two. It covers Israel, India, Persia, Phoenicia, and the minor nations of western Asia. The plan of the set was to let the historians of each age speak in their own words, arranged into one continuous story. Sets like this one filled the shelves of public libraries and prosperous homes. Volume two gives the ancient Near East as scholars of 1905 understood it, built from sources old and new and revised by specialists in each field.
54037-the-seaside-sibyl-or-leaves-of-des:
The Seaside Sibyl, or Leaves of Destiny is a fortune teller in verse, in an American edition copyrighted in April eighteen eighty two by E S Wells of Jersey City. The slim pamphlet cost five cents in its first edition. Ads for Rough on Rats poison fill the front pages. Wells made that rat poison and sold it in fifteen and twenty five cent boxes.

Verse fortunes in the pamphlet treat love, marriage, and fate in short rhymes. One piece, The Sibyl Cure, holds that for love there is but one cure. The lover must resign himself to marry, or pine. Cheap print of this kind sold at resorts and by druggists in that age. Readers get a neat case of verse, fate, and sales craft bound in one small package.
54143-english-lands-letters-and-kings-vo:
Donald Mitchell closed his four-part survey of English lands and letters with this volume, published in 1897. It covers the years from the later Georges to Queen Victoria. Mitchell calls his short opening note a forecast and a menu, meant to remind old readers of the series and tempt new ones at the bookshop.

The tour starts in the Lake District, among hills and waters linked with Wordsworth. Southey, De Quincey and Professor Wilson appear there, full of strong talk and odd habits. Later stops reach Crabbe Robinson in London and the Tweed banks of Scott's Abbotsford, mixing place, writers and kings in an easy, gossipy walk.
54240-proceedings-of-the-california-acad:
The California Academy of Sciences printed this volume of its Proceedings in San Francisco in 1906. It is volume four of the third series, on zoology, covering work from 1905 and 1906. The index alone runs to many pages of Latin names.

The papers treat the reptiles and amphibians of California and nearby lands. Rattlesnakes, lizards, and salamanders fill most entries. One paper reports the leatherback turtle on the California coast. Another notes the spotted night snake in the state's center. A short study asks about the shape of the pupil in one snake genus. The volume is a working record of western field science, built name by name.
55195-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
The Historians' History of the World is a vast narrative of the rise and growth of nations, in twenty five volumes. It was recorded, its title says, by over two thousand great writers of all ages. Henry Smith Williams edited it with a board of advisers, and it appeared in 1904 at New York and London. Volume three, hosted here, treats Greece to the Peloponnesian War.

A portrait of Herodotus fronts the volume. The board of contributors spans the learned world: Erman of Berlin, Halevy of Paris, Cheyne of Oxford, and Meyer of Berlin stand among them. Professors from Budapest, Vienna, and Tokyo add their names. The plan was to let the great historians themselves tell the story, age by age, in their own words, stitched by editors. This volume walks Greece from its dawn to the great war between Athens and Sparta, through the eyes of its classic tellers.
55497-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
The Historians' History of the World is a twenty-five-volume narrative of the rise and development of nations, edited by Henry Smith Williams and issued in 1904. The volume shown here is volume four, Greece to the Roman Conquest. Its title page boasts that the story is recorded by over two thousand of the great writers of all ages. A board of distinguished advisers and contributors assisted the editor.

The contributors list reads like a roll of the universities of two continents. Professors from Berlin, Oxford, Paris, Vienna, Harvard, Columbia, and Michigan appear among the editorial revisers. A portrait of the historian Grote fronts this volume. A transcriber's note warns of editorial slips in the original, where some reference letters lack matching entries in the reference lists.
57159-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Henry Smith Williams edited The Historians' History of the World, a set in twenty-five volumes printed in New York and London in 1904. Volume five, The Roman Republic, is this book. A print of Livy, the Roman writer, fronts the set's title page.

The set tells the rise and growth of nations in the words of more than two thousand great writers of all ages. A board of famed scholars from Berlin, Paris, Oxford, and more helped shape the work. This volume walks Rome from city state to republic in the words of those who told it best. Students get a vast, rich tome of Roman days.
58124-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Volume Six of The Historians History of the World covers the early Roman Empire. Henry Smith Williams shaped the whole twenty five volume set, which came out in 1904. The set retells the rise and growth of nations in the words of more than two thousand great writers of all ages.

A large board of advisers and scholars from Berlin, Paris, Oxford, and other seats of learning helped with the work. This volume takes Rome from its imperial start through its early rulers and wars. The method lets past masters speak in their own words, tied into one tale. Readers get both a story of Rome and a taste of how the best past writers told it. The set aimed to put a whole library of history in one home.
58315-history-of-the-fifty-seventh-regim:
Five men of the regiment, Martin, Strouss, Madge, Campbell, and Zahniser, compiled this history of the Fifty-Seventh Regiment, Pennsylvania Veteran Volunteer Infantry. The regiment served in the Army of the Potomac, first in the Third Corps and later in the Second. The book is dedicated to the members of the Fifty-Seventh, living and dead, and to their children and grandchildren.

The chapters follow the regiment from Camp Curtin and the march to Washington through the Peninsula campaign, Williamsburg, and Fair Oaks. Then come the Seven Days, the second Bull Run campaign, Fredericksburg, and Chancellorsville. At Gettysburg the regiment fought on July 2, and General Graham was wounded and captured. Strength and losses are stated for each action, as these regimental histories usually do.
59134-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Volume Seven of The Historians History of the World covers the later Roman Empire. Henry Smith Williams shaped the whole twenty five volume set, which came out in 1904. A front print shows Gibbon, the famed writer on Romes fall.

The set retells the rise and growth of nations in the words of more than two thousand great writers of all ages. Scholars from Berlin, Paris, Oxford, Vienna, and other seats of learning helped shape the text. This volume follows Rome as its power waned and its lands split and fell. Readers can hear how Gibbon and other masters framed that long decline. The book suits readers who want Romes last age told by the classic voices on it.
59352-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
Merle d'Aubigné, the Swiss church historian, wrote the History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin as a sequel to his famous history of the earlier Reformation. This file holds the first volume. A French motto on the title page sets his theme: in Christ's reign only the new man flourishes.

D'Aubigné writes Geneva's story as sacred drama: Calvin's city, its councils, its refugees, and its reach across France, Scotland, and the Netherlands. His narrative method, learned from the great French historians, puts the reader inside consistories and studies. English and American Protestants devoured the volumes as they appeared. The history is partisan and proud of it, and its documentary wealth keeps it on shelves its theology no longer commands.
60035-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin, in its fourth part of eight, is the great church tale of a famed Swiss hand. He had writ a past tale of the change of faith in the age past. Two quotes in French from the great man him self head the part.

It came out at New York in the mid eighteen sixties. Its word at the front tells its span for this part. It tells the deeds of a big age in the change in five lands: England, Geneva, France, the German states, and Italy. From the first, its hand aimed at a tale of the whole change in Europe, as its name shows. Some, mis led by that name, are set right there.
60152-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin, volume two, is by the Swiss historian Merle d'Aubigné. Longman published the London edition in 1863. The volume is subtitled Geneva and France. Its motto, in French, is a saying of Calvin's: in the reign of Christ only the new man flourishes and has vigour. D'Aubigné had already written the well-known history of the Reformation of the sixteenth century.

The contents open Book Two, France in favourable times. Chapter thirteen follows John Calvin as a student at the University of Orleans in 1527 and 1528. His friend there, the students of Orleans, and Pierre de l'Etoile fill the summary. Calvin was received in the Picard nation of students and nominated proctor. Later summaries show him supplying another's place, sought as a teacher, and seeking a hiding-place for study.
60708-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, volume four, continues the history of Joseph Smith, the Prophet, by himself. Roberts supplied an introduction and notes, and the Church published the volume at Salt Lake City in 1908. This is Period One of the history, drawn from the Prophet's own record. A portrait frontispiece and full chapter summaries guide the reader.

The first chapter covers the departure of the Twelve for England and the healing of the sick at Commerce, Illinois. It prints discourses by the brothers Pratt and minutes of the October 1839 conference. The second chapter follows the Prophet's journey to Washington. There the Saints petitioned Congress for redress of the wrongs inflicted on them in Missouri. It gives affidavits on Missouri affairs and the Prophet's letters reporting the state of things at Washington.
60736-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints published this fifth volume of its history at Salt Lake City in 1909. The core text is Joseph Smith's own history, told by himself, with an introduction and notes by Roberts. This volume covers the Nauvoo years, the church's city on the Mississippi.

Contents treat the perfidy of John Bennett, once mayor of Nauvoo, and the attempted killing of Governor Boggs of Missouri. Missouri twice tried to seize Smith and carry him back for trial. Notes also date the revelation on the eternity of the marriage covenant. Readers get the Saints' own record of their most dramatic years, with the prophet at the center.
60758-history-of-the-church-of-jesus-chr:
Volume six of the History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints came from the Church at Salt Lake City in 1912. It holds the History of Joseph Smith by himself, with an introduction and notes by Roberts. The contents map the Nauvoo years. They tell why the Saints were welcomed to Illinois. They also show how Nauvoo rose as a possible center of manufactures.

School measures, jealousy of Nauvoo's fast greatness, and the character of its founder fill the survey. These pages run toward the storm that would kill Smith and drive his people west. The set is the standard documentary history of early Mormonism. Readers get the prophet's own account, framed by his church's scholar.
60774-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
Volume three of the History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin, by Merle d’Aubigne, continues his great narrative. Spottiswoode of London printed the English edition of the work. D’Aubigne wrote as a Swiss Protestant historian of strong faith. His history ran through many volumes on either side of this one.

Calvin at Geneva stands at the centre of the age he treats. Kings, reformers, and martyrs fill the crowded stage of his pages. D’Aubigne writes with a preacher’s fire and a scholar’s heap of records. Victorian parlours took his volumes as both history and devotion. The Reformation is told here as a drama of conscience against power. This middle volume carries the tale through Calvin’s hardest years.
61277-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
J H Merle d'Aubigné continued his history of the Reformation with this fifth volume of the second series. Robert Carter published it at New York in 1876. The volume treats England, Geneva, and Ferrara in the time of Calvin.

The preface sets the frame. The first series ran from the start of the movement to the Confession of Augsburg in 1530. The second runs on toward the triumph of the cause in land after land. D'Aubigné draws a line he will not cross. His subject is the Reformation itself, he says, not the later history of Protestantism as a party.
6155-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-v:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's fifth book runs from Cimon's death in 449 BC to Pericles's death in the third year of the Peloponnesian War, 429 BC. Thucydides, chosen by the aristocratic party to oppose Pericles, opens the book, with his policy, Pericles's munificence, the sacred war, and Coronea.

Revolt of Euboea and Megara, invasion and retreat of Peloponnesians, reduction of Euboea, punishment of Histiaea, and a thirty years' truce follow, with Thucydides ostracized. On Cimon's death the aristocrats needed a home leader, not a distant general, to meet Pericles in assembly and intrigue. This book alone is described here.
61913-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
The Rev J H Merle D'Aubigne wrote a history of the Reformation in the time of Calvin. Robert Carter and Brothers issued Volume Seven in New York. William L R Cates turned the work into English for the set. The volume treats England, Geneva, France, Germany, and Italy.

A warm review by Professor F Godet of Neuchatel fronts the hosted form. Godet praises true history over religious novels for feeding faith with fact. Martyrs, stakes, and trials stand as real events, not invented scenes. Church readers gain a grave, stirring survey of faith under fire.
6261-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A village lies in a valley once the bed of a great river, in days when Ireland, Wales, and Brittany were joined and the Thames flowed into the Seine. For generations it has lived serenely, never knowing turmoil. Three buildings stand out. A square red brick mansion sits behind a high wall. A low ivy covered house, once a monastery and called the Cloistered House, stands beside a plain wooden hall with heavy oak doors and diamond panes.

This opening part, Book One, follows David Claridge as the spirit moves him, through the gates of the world, banishment, and a call that pulls him from Hamley toward Egypt. His grandfather Luke watches forces stir in the boy that Claridge blood did not plant. Parker writes a quiet English valley first, so that the wider world, when it comes, breaks on a peace the reader has learned to love.
6262-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Months later, a letter reaches David Claridge in Cairo from Faith Claridge in Hamley, asking if he still loves the village people who once gave him sour bread. She tells of Kimber, the man David struck at a public house, who followed to London the lass David kissed and begged her to marry him. Refused at first with anger, she promised an answer in three years if he stayed sober and hard working meanwhile.

This part of the novel, Book Two, widens David's way from Hamley to Cairo, through a compact, a letter, a night, and a woman, and on to a jehad and lions. Four people know a secret, a ropemaking man strikes, and the tale passes beyond the pale. Parker sets a Quaker village voice against Egyptian courts, where Nahoum rises and David's face, white at the palace, hides a deeper game.
6263-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Faith raises her eyes from a paper and talks with Soolsby, who rests his chin on a chair he is caning and smiles with suppressed amusement. Three years have passed since a promise was made. Soolsby would drink no more until David's return, and Faith counts the time as an old memory, though she calls herself almost an old woman now. Soolsby answers that time is afraid of her and lets her be.

This part, Book Three, opens with Soolsby's hand upon the curtain and runs through debt and accounting, a woman of the crossroads, time the idol breaker, and sharper than a sword. Old antagonism flares again, one strong will resenting another, as if the world held no room for both. Parker writes Hamley waiting and Egypt working, with Faith at the centre, patient, watchful, and far from passive.
6264-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Higli Pasha laughs to himself in a courtyard of Nahoum Pasha's palace, narghileh stem in mouth, waiting for its owner with hilarious patience. Years have changed him little since the expedition against southern tribes that followed David's appointment to office. Diaz died of a tarantula bite, Higli took a slight wound and retreated safely to Cairo, and of the old conspirators only Nahoum and Higli remain, never partners in any true sense.

This part, Book Four, turns Nahoum's screw, with a recoil, a move by Lacey, a struggle in the desert, forty stripes save one, and a dark indenture. Nahoum at last drops his mask, and Prince Kaid's dark face turns on old friends. Parker writes palace intrigue as a slow tightening, where laughter in a courtyard can sit beside ruin, and a man's past bargains return to claim him.
6265-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A tenor voice rings out in an opera house, singing words about souls in purgatory and a plea not to be forgotten. The sound finds far recesses of feeling in its hearers. Women of poise and social fame drop their eyes to opera glasses and programmes, recalling first married days and seals of devotion long since lost with fresh desires. Young lovers, happy and defiant in each other, are suddenly arrested by a music that speaks of a tragic Italian tale.

This part, Book Five, runs from the flight of the wounded through a flying shuttle, Jasper Kimber speaking, and Faith journeying to London. A woman pauses, moves on with purpose, and finds an opened letter on the floor whose first words scorch her eyes. Parker writes opera night as a mirror, where art stirs private memory and a single letter can turn a life.
6266-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Hylda wakes, as it were, upon a scene unchanged, brilliant and full of colour, a chaos of decoration and noisy streams of life. Craftsmen crowd dark bazaars, merchants haggle on benches, hawkers cry their wares, and a people live upon the streets while houses seem empty. Sais run before a Pasha's carriage, donkey boys shriek for the right of way, and camels force a calm passage through swirling crowds.

This closing part, Book Six, sends Hylda to seek Nahoum, then into the land of Shinar and onto the loom of destiny. Word comes up the Nile, a wounded Arab is carried in with blood on his face, and David's face clouds at news he should have had sooner. Parker ends his long tale of England and Egypt with a city in full noise and a reckoning that has travelled fifty years to arrive.
62913-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
Volume eight of D'Aubigne's History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin is presented in the publisher's pages as the completion of the work. The eight volumes are priced at sixteen dollars the set, beside the five volumes on the sixteenth century at six. Review clippings fill the front of the book.

The New York Observer calls the history one of the grandest literary and historical works of this or any age, a romance in fascination with the weight of sound research. The North Christian Advocate, thirty years after the first volumes, finds the same clear, forcible style, maturer and richer. The Chronicle praises the copious notes, and the Christian Instructor the pleasure and profit of the reading.
63489-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Historians History of the World, volume eight, covers Parthians, Sassanids, and Arabs. Henry Smith Williams edited the twenty five volume set with a wide board. The Outlook Company of New York and the History Association issued it in nineteen o four. Over two thousand great writers of all ages supply the narrative matter.

Advisers named include Adolf Erman, Joseph Halevy, and Thomas Cheyne of Oxford. Andrew McLaughlin, David Muller, Alfred Rambaud, and Eduard Meyer aid the board. Theodor Noldeke, Albert Hart, and James Shotwell add their learning to it. The Crusades and the Papacy share this volume with the eastern empires. Portraits of scholars like Noldeke illustrate the stately reference set.
65984-history-of-the-reformation-in-euro:
Volume six of Merle d'Aubigne's History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin covers Scotland, Switzerland, and Geneva. Cates translated it, and Robert Carter and Brothers published it at New York in 1877. A French saying of Calvin stands at the front: in the reign of Christ, only the new man is flourishing and has vigour.
