The preface reports that the author died at Geneva on October 21, 1872, with only a few chapters left to write.

D'Aubigne's great history told the Reformation as a drama of faith, from a warm Protestant sympathy. His Calvin volumes carry the story into the reformer's own city and into Knox's Scotland. English readers took their Reformation largely from him.
66490-the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bie:
Tangential Views is the ninth volume of the collected works of Ambrose Bierce, issued at New York and Washington in 1911. The edition ran to two hundred and fifty numbered sets, autographed by the author. The volume gathers short essays and sketches. Titles include Some Privations of the Coming Man, The Civilization of the Monkey, and John Smith's Ancestors.

Other pieces treat the religion of the table, the art of controversy, and the decay of the American foot. Newspapers, actors, truth, sleep, and modern warfare all fall under Bierce's dry eye. One essay opens with a German physician's solemn view that civilized man is losing his sense of smell through disuse. Bierce grants it, and adds that our duller noses suit a world richer in bad odours. These views show the famed wit at his most cutting, in short prose pieces from his newspaper years.
66694-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
The tenth volume of The Historians' History of the World is given to Spain and Portugal. Henry Smith Williams edited the twenty-five volumes, issued by the Outlook Company at New York and the History Association at London in 1905. The plan was grand: a narrative of the rise and development of nations as recorded by over two thousand of the great writers of all ages. A distinguished board of advisers and contributors, from Berlin, Oxford, Paris, and Harvard, stands at the front.

The Spain and Portugal part rests chiefly on named authorities: Mariana, Prescott, Zurita, Herculano, and Dozy among them. Prescott's portrait fronts the volume, a fair emblem of its method, since his Ferdinand and Isabella set the English-speaking world's Spain. The series sold history as a library, one nation at a time, in the historians' own words. Volume Ten carries the Peninsula from its early kingdoms toward empire.
67505-the-life-of-clara-barton-founder-o:
The first volume of a biography of Clara Barton by William E Barton. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1922. The author was a distant kinsman, not her descendant. He dedicates the book to her trusted nephew Stephen. Twenty chapters carry this volume to the lecture platform. Her unpublished autobiography supplies whole sections.

Clara Barton's first autobiography attempt came late, in 1876. Susan B Anthony had asked for a sketch for an encyclopedia of women. Barton laboured long over her reply, the biographer notes. Schoolroom years and the Patent Office precede the war. Harper's Ferry to Antietam brings her to the front. Andersonville and its aftermath close the war record here. The American Red Cross still waits in volume two.
67847-memoirs-and-posthumous-works-of-ma:
Volume 1 of the Memoirs and Posthumous Works of Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was printed in Dublin in 1798. The memoirs are by William Godwin, who argues that giving the public an account of a person of eminent merit is a duty owed by survivors. Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, had died the year before. The volume joins the life to her letters, including letters on the character of the French nation and on the management of infants, and her letters to her publisher, Mr Johnson.

Godwin's candor about her life shocked the age and shadowed her name for a century. Read today, the memoirs are both a pioneering biography and the record of a radical marriage of minds. The Dublin printing spread the book through Ireland in the year of the rebellion.
67954-the-life-of-clara-barton-founder-o:
William Barton, a relative and minister, wrote this life of Clara Barton, founder of the American Red Cross, in two volumes printed at Boston in 1922. This file holds the second volume. A portrait shows Clara Barton at eighty. The contents begin with her first knowledge of the Red Cross.

Chapters follow her through the Franco Prussian war and the illness that followed it. The forerunners of the Red Cross, the years of lonely struggle, and the birth of the American society come next, then the trials of a treaty and the perils of success. Barton in Cuba, her retirement, her religion, and her last years close the life. The author shared her name and had her papers, and the biography is the standard family account.
69073-the-uncivilized-races-of-men-in-al:
Wood gathered this large survey, issued in Hartford in 1877 as volume one of two. Wood says travellers had left accounts of distant peoples scattered through many scarce and costly books. His task was to bring those reports together in one ordered work on manners, customs and daily life around the world.

The many plates were drawn from photos and from sketches by travellers, some made for this book. Wood thanks men such as Baines for help and first-hand skill. Readers should note the dated terms and views of its age, but the volume shows how Victorian readers pictured peoples far from modern city life.
69074-the-uncivilized-races-of-men-in-al:
The Uncivilized Races of Men in All Countries of the World, volume two of two, is a survey by the Reverend J G Wood, printed at Hartford in 1877. The title page promises a full account of the manners and customs of its peoples, and of their physical, social, mental, moral, and religious characteristics. New designs by Angas, Danby, Wolf, and Zwecker illustrate the work.

This volume runs from chapter seventy-six to chapter one hundred and seventy, with more than two hundred pictures. Its preface says the volume treats the tribes of America and of the islands between that coast and Asia. The contents, list of illustrations, and index are printed in both volumes for ease of reference. Wood thanks the Geographical and Anthropological Societies for access to their libraries. His survey belongs to the Victorian age of popular ethnology.
70547-parodies-of-the-works-of-english-a:
Parodies of the Works of English and American Authors, volume five, is an anthology collected and annotated by Walter Hamilton, published in London by Reeves and Turner in 1888. Hamilton wrote on patriotic songs, George Cruikshank, and the poets laureate. A motto from Montaigne calls the book a nosegay of culled flowers.

The volume's centrepiece is parodies of Gray's Elegy in a Country Churchyard, with other poems. Cowper, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Lewis, Leigh Hunt, Macaulay, Thackeray, Shelley, and Mrs Browning all receive imitations. National songs of the United States, modern American poets, and songs of the Civil War close the list. Hamilton meant the set to stand as a book of reference on parody and burlesque. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
71209-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Volume nine of The Historians History of the World treats Italy. Henry Smith Williams shaped the set, and the Outlook Company printed this volume in New York in 1905, under a 1904 copyright. A portrait of Macchiavelli stands at the front. A board of advisers and helpers from many lands backed the work.

The names run from Adolf Erman of Berlin and Joseph Halevy of the College of France to Thomas K Cheyne of Oxford. Andrew C McLaughlin of Michigan, David H Muller of Vienna, and Alfred Rambaud of Paris stand with them. Eduard Meyer of Berlin and James T Shotwell of Columbia close the list shown. Italy tale runs from Rome rise through the city states to a united kingdom, told in the words of the great historians. Each volume treats one land or age.
72686-fornander-collection-of-hawaiian-a:
Abraham Fornander, a Swedish judge and scholar in Hawaii, gathered this great store of Hawaiian antiquities and folk lore from original sources. This volume came out at Honolulu in 1916 and 1917 as part of the memoirs of the Bishop Museum. Thomas Thrum edited the translations and added notes and pictures.

The first part gives the Hawaiians' own account of the forming of their islands and the origin of their race. Chapters tell the birth of the islands, the story of Wakea, and the genealogies of chiefs, name by name. Fornander took the tales down from Hawaiian tellers in their own tongue. The collection is a base record of a people's memory of itself.
73166-fornander-collection-of-hawaiian-a:
Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk Lore gathers old Hawaiian tradition from first sources. Abraham Fornander collected the tales, and Thrum edited the English versions with notes. The Bishop Museum at Honolulu printed volume five in nineteen eighteen to nineteen nineteen. It forms the second series of the museum's memoirs on Polynesian study.

The title promises the Hawaiians' own account of their islands' making and their migrations. Part one opens with the legend of Kawelo, a fighting chief of Kauai. His birth, his fame on Oahu, and his wars fill ten chapters of deeds. The story of Pakaa, keeper of the wind gourd Laamaomao, follows next. His son Kuapakaa chants the winds of each island to a voyaging king. Storms swamp the canoes when the boy frees the winds at last.
73369-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Henry Smith Williams edited this vast history of the world in twenty-five volumes, published in New York and London in 1905. Its plan was bold: a narrative of the rise of nations as recorded by over two thousand great writers of all ages. Hume's portrait stands near this volume's front.

Volume seventeen finishes Switzerland and takes up Russia and Poland. The words of the historians themselves, chosen and linked by the editors, do the telling. A distinguished board of advisers helped shape the whole. Readers get the nineteenth century's grand idea of history, one volume of twenty-five at a time.
73600-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for March 1854, number 461 of volume seventy-five, opens with a biography of Disraeli at page 255. The Quiet Heart follows in its fourth part, then the Russian Church and the protectorate in Turkey, a burning question on the edge of the Crimean War. The Two Arnolds, Count Sigismund's Will, and news from the farm fill the middle of the number.

Alexander Smith's poems get their review, and the epidemics of the Middle Ages their essay. A song and the new reform bill close the list. Maga, as its readers called it, was the wittiest and most Tory of the great monthlies. Readers get a whole number of it, politics, tales, and verse in the true Edinburgh blend.
74570-fornander-collection-of-hawaiian-a:
Volume six of the Fornander Collection gathers Hawaiian antiquities and folk-lore. The Bishop Museum at Honolulu printed it in 1919 and 1920. Abraham Fornander collected the texts from original sources. Thomas Thrum edited the translations and added notes. Part one treats old religious ceremonies. Heathen prayers and the building of temples follow.

A long history of the Hawaiian priesthood fills many pages. It covers sorcery, divination, weather prophets, and healing priests. Omens from clouds, rainbows, and birds are explained. Fornander spent a lifetime recording Hawaiian tradition. This volume holds the sacred side of that record. A core text for Pacific studies.
77058-the-historians-history-of-the-worl:
Historians History of the World, volume eleven, covers France from 843 to 1715 in narrative form. Henry Smith Williams edited the twenty five volume set with a board of advisers. The Outlook Company of New York and the History Association of London issued it in 1905. Over two thousand great writers of all ages supply the recorded narrative.

Contributors and editorial revisers include scholars such as Erman of Berlin on the board. Transcriber notes flag reference letters in the original lacking matches in the lists. France from the Carolingian split to the age of Louis the Fourteenth fills this volume. General readers of 1905 gained world history woven from the historians own words.
9598-criticism-part-4-from-the-works-of-:
Part four of Whittier's Criticism holds his essays on poems and poets, led by a review of Longfellow's Evangeline. Whittier hails it as an American poem at last, telling the sad exile of Acadian settlers from Minas Basin. He praises its pictures of farm life, Indian summer, and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. The range runs from Nova Scotia to the Gulf of Mexico.

Other essays in the part take up mirth and medicine, fame and glory, fanaticism, and the poetry of the North. Whittier judges as a poet and a moralist at once. A reader gets a critic's view of his age's verse, warm toward Longfellow and sharp on what makes poetry last.
9760-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book five of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, opens with the great battle. Dawn breaks on a night of ruin, and the Moors on Granada's walls see Ferdinand's whole army marching to assault. Burned camp wrecks lie behind, while pennons wave and trumpets sound ahead. The Moors, hoping for a Christian retreat, fill with alarm.

King Boabdil, at the head of his guards, rallies his men as the assault breaks. Lytton stages the siege's climax with pageantry and dread. A reader gets the final battle book of a Granada romance, where a kingdom's fate hangs on one morning's fight.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: William Henry Harrison and his successors fill this fourth volume compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume spans eight years from 1841 to 1849, covering Harrison, Tyler, and Polk. It opens with the first succession of a vice president after a president's death. Richardson presents the official record of a turbulent period in American history.
a-dark-month-from-swinburne-s-collected-: Algernon Charles Swinburne's fifth volume gathers studies in song, a century of roundels, and sonnets on English dramatic poets. The volume also includes the Heptalogia and other pieces from his middle period. A Dark Month stands among these collected poems of varied form and theme. Swinburne's rich music and classical learning run through the whole selection.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-v:
The fifth tome of Barbier de Meynard's Les Prairies d'Or appeared in 1869, midway in the nine-tome French set. Its author, al-Masudi of Baghdad, finished the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems, in the last years of his life. He had spent decades on the roads and seas of Asia and Africa.

Few medieval books hold so much. The science of the earth, the tales of ancient kings, and the ways of Hindus, Persians, and Franks all stand beside the chronicle of the caliphs. Al-Masudi wrote to teach and to delight at once. The French editors add notes on the hard names and places. This middle tome carries the reader deep into the whole.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-v:
Book V of Athens: Its Rise and Fall, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, covers a famous span. It runs from the death of Cimon in 449 BC. It ends with the death of Pericles in 429, in the Peloponnesian War's third year. The aristocratic party, Lytton begins, needed a new kind of leader after Cimon. No dazzling general absent on distant expeditions would do. They needed a statesman. He must meet Pericles in the assembly with equal civil experience and oratorical talent. Their choice fell on Thucydides, Cimon's brother in law.

His policy and Pericles' public munificence fill the first movement. A sacred war and revolts follow. The ostracism of Thucydides leaves Pericles supreme. The book closes over the plague years and the great man's death.
britannica-1911-alexius-v:
Alexius V held the eastern Roman throne only while Constantinople fought for its life. His full name ran Alexius Ducas Murtzuphlos, and he was kin to the imperial house of the Angeli. A rising inside the city raised him on 5 February 1204, as the Latins of the Fourth Crusade pressed their siege. The revolt had thrown down Isaac II and Alexius IV.

Defence of the city fell to Alexius, and he led it with great courage until, on 12 April, no hope remained. He then ran from the city. He sought to join Alexius III in a stand against the Latins, but the former emperor had him blinded instead. Crusaders caught him next and killed him by throwing him off the Pillar of Theodosius, as the slayer of Alexius IV.
britannica-1911-baldwin-v:
Baldwin V was the child king of Jerusalem from 1183 to 1186. He was the son of Sibylla, daughter of Amalric I, by her first husband, William of Montferrat. Too young to rule, he held the crown in name only, under the regency of Raymund of Tripoli.

The 1911 Britannica entry is very short, and it keeps to the bare facts of the reign. Two points stand out in it. Saladin was advancing against the kingdom from outside. At the same time, quarrels split the court at home, above all the strife between the government and Guy of Lusignan, Sibylla's second husband.
britannica-1911-clement-clement-v:
Clement the Fifth was pope from 1305 to 1314, born Bertrand de Gouth of a noble Gascon family. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his study of arts at Toulouse and law at Orleans and Bologna. Canon posts at Bordeaux and service to his archbishop brother came in turn. Boniface the Eighth made him a chaplain and then bishop of Cominges in 1295.

In 1299 he rose to archbishop of Bordeaux under that same pope. His presence at a Rome synod in 1302 marked him as a Boniface man. Yet the French court held no grudge against him for that stance. At Perugia in June 1305 the cardinals chose him to end an eleven month deadlock.
britannica-1911-frederick-v:
Frederick V (1596-1632), elector palatine of the Rhine and king of Bohemia, was born at Amberg on 26 August 1596, son of Frederick IV. He became elector in 1610 under a guardian, came of age in 1614, and in 1613 had married Elizabeth, daughter of James I of England. He headed the Evangelical Union his father had founded.

In August 1619 the Bohemian estates deposed Ferdinand and chose Frederick as king, and he was crowned at Prague on 4 November. Four days later his forces were routed at the White Hill by Tilly, and the short reign ended. Mocked as the Winter King, he fled to the Netherlands, and in 1623 his electorate passed to Maximilian of Bavaria. He died at Mainz in 1632. His son Charles Louis regained the Palatinate in 1648, and his daughter Sophia was mother of George I.
britannica-1911-john-vi-or-v:
John VI or V (c. 1292–1383), surnamed Cantacuzene, was East Roman emperor, born at Constantinople and linked to the house of Palaeologus through his mother. Under Andronicus III he held the chief conduct of affairs from 1328. When the emperor died in 1341, Cantacuzene was left regent for the boy John Palaeologus.

Suspected by the empress and fought by a strong court party, he had himself crowned emperor at Didymoteichos. Six years of civil war followed, and both sides called in Serbs, Turks, and hired troops. With Turkish aid he entered Constantinople in 1347 and became joint emperor. Wars with Genoa and Serbia strained the shrunken empire. The Turks made their first lasting foothold in Europe at Callipolis in 1354. Late that year John Palaeologus retook the capital. Cantacuzene withdrew to a monastery, took the name Joasaph Christodulus, and wrote a history of 1320 to 1356 that defends his own acts.
britannica-1911-ladislaus-v:
Ladislaus V (1440–1457), king of Hungary and Bohemia, was the son of Albert of Hungary and Elizabeth, daughter of the emperor Sigismund. He was born at Komárom on the 22nd of February 1440, four months after his father's death — hence Ladislaus Posthumus. His mother had the holy crown stolen from its guardians at Visegrad and the infant crowned at Székesfehérvár on the 15th of May 1440. She then placed him under his uncle, the emperor Frederick III.

When Wladislaus III died in 1444 the Hungarian estates elected Ladislaus, but Frederick gave up the child and the crown only in 1452. The boy then passed to Ulrich Cillei, who filled him with hatred of the Hunyadis. He was crowned king of Bohemia on the 28th of October 1453. Careless of the Turkish danger, he hampered Hunyadi's plans and fled the country at the news of the siege of Belgrade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-v:
Alexander V, born Pietro Philarghi about 1339 on Crete, was elected pope on 26 June 1409 and died at Bologna on 3 May 1410. Homeless and begging in a Cretan city, with neither parents nor relations known, he found a patron in a discerning Capuchin friar. The friar gave him an elementary education and guided him into the Franciscan order. At Paris he shone as professor, preacher, and writer, and wrote a commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard.

Returning to Italy, Philarghi served the Duke of Milan as tutor and ambassador. He rose through Piacenza, Vicenza, and Navoya to Archbishop of Milan in 1402, and became cardinal in 1405 and papal legate to Lombardy. He championed a council to end the Great Schism, and the cardinals chose him unanimously to fill the papal chair, presumably vacant. His ten-month pontificate was spent in failed efforts to reach Rome, then held by King Ladislas of Naples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-v:
Boniface V, a Neapolitan pope from 619 to 625, is remembered as the mildest of men, devoted above all to his clergy. He followed Deusdedit after the see stood empty for more than a year, and was consecrated on 23 December 619. Before his consecration, Italy had been shaken by the revolt of Eleutherius, exarch of Ravenna, who was slain by his own troops before reaching Rome.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with rules on sanctuary rights, wills, and the duties of acolytes, who could not displace deacons at baptism in the Lateran. He completed and consecrated the cemetery of Saint Nicomedes. Bede records his affectionate letters to England, urging King Edwin of Northumbria toward the faith and Queen Ethelberga to work for her husband's conversion. He was buried in Saint Peter's on 25 October 625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emperor-charl:
Charles V, also Charles I of Spain, was the Habsburg ruler over whom the sun was said never to set, born at Ghent in 1500 and dead at Yuste in 1558. Son of Philip of Burgundy and Joanna, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, he inherited Burgundy in 1506. His aunt Margaret of Austria held the regency while he was a minor. Adrian of Utrecht, his teacher at Louvain, left a deep mark on his mind.

Declared of age in January 1515, he sought peace with France through the treaties of Paris in 1515 and Noyon in 1516. On Ferdinand of Aragon's death in 1516 he claimed Spain, took the title King of Castile, and reached Spain in the autumn of 1517, despite a popular brother Ferdinand. Power left to Burgundian favourites, above all Chievres, provoked the rising of the Comunidades. Later parts follow his election as emperor, his long wars, and his abdication at Yuste.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-v:
Felix V was the antipope elected by the Council of Basle. Born Amadeus VIII of Savoy in 1383, he had retired to a semi-monastic life at Ripaille. The council, having deposed Eugene IV, chose the rich and powerful duke in 1439. He accepted in 1440 and was solemnly crowned at Basle that July.

Felix found recognition only in Savoy, Switzerland, and a few German lands. Many named cardinals refused the dignity he offered them. He quarrelled with Basle over revenues and rights for several years. In 1449 he submitted to Nicholas V and became Cardinal of St Sabina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-v:
Henry V, German king and Roman emperor, was born in 1081 as son of Henry IV and died at Utrecht in 1125. Described as crafty, sullen, and harsh, he nevertheless defended crown rights with prudence and energy. He took the throne by a compact with the papacy and the princes, his father's bitterest opponents. Yet at once he adopted his father's policy, refusing above all to surrender investiture, the royal right over the German Church.

In 1110 Henry marched to Rome for his imperial coronation. There Paschal II proposed that bishops surrender all worldly possessions in return for the king abandoning investiture. The German princes rejected the scheme, Henry seized the pope and forced his demands, and excommunications followed. Defeated in Saxony in 1115 and crowned emperor at St. Peter's in 1117, he finally reached the Concordat of Worms in 1122, distinguishing ecclesiastical office from temporal possessions and ending the great investiture controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-v:
Pope Adrian V, Genoa-born Ottobuono Fieschi, nephew of Innocent IV, held the papacy only briefly in 1276. Viterbo elected him 12 July 1276. While still Cardinal Fieschi he had worked to mend relations in England between Henry III and the barons in revolt.

Once pope he cancelled Gregory X's strict conclave rules, but death on 18 August cut short his plan to replace them with gentler ones. He survived barely long enough, the entry says, to sense the weight of the papal mantle. Dante gives him a memorable dialogue in Purgatory, canto nineteen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict V, birth date unknown, died 4 July 965. Romans chose him pope in May 964 at a perilous moment. Otto I had deposed the unworthy John XII by force and set up his own man, Leo VIII. At their first chance the Romans threw Leo out, and when John XII died 14 May 964 they chose Cardinal-Deacon Benedict, famed for learning as Grammaticus.

Otto raged, marched on Rome, seized Benedict, and closed his pontificate 23 June 964. More likely Benedict was stripped of office by force than that he freely called himself an intruder. Having restored Leo, Otto took Benedict to Germany. Adaldag, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, treated him with great kindness, and some German clergy still honoured him as pope. His body, first laid at Hamburg, later moved to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-bl-urban:
Pope Blessed Urban V, born Guillaume de Grimoard at Grisac in Languedoc in 1310, reigned from 1362 to 1370 from Avignon. Educated at Montpellier and Toulouse, he became a Benedictine monk at Chirac. He was professed at Saint Victor in Marseilles, whose love for his order he kept even as pope, still wearing its habit. He took his doctorate in 1342 and became one of the greatest canonists of his day.

He taught canon law at Montpellier, Toulouse, Paris, and Avignon. He served as vicar-general of Clermont and Uzès, then became abbot of Saint Germain d'Auxerre's priory and of Saint Victor in 1361. His diplomatic missions to Milan, Italy, and Naples marked him out. The cardinals, deadlocked by jealousy, chose this non-cardinal for virtue, learning, and practical skill. He was consecrated on 6 November 1362, taking the name Urban because, as he said, all earlier Urbans had been saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin:
Pope Celestine V, born Pietro di Murrone in 1215 in the Neapolitan province of Molise, was the hermit-pope who abdicated after five months. He became a Benedictine at seventeen and was ordained at Rome, then sought solitude on Monte Morone and the wilder Majella, modelling himself on the Baptist. His hair-shirt was knotted, an iron chain ringed his wasted frame, and he fasted daily except Sunday, keeping four Lents a year, three on bread and water.

Kindred spirits gathered around him until thirty-six monasteries with six hundred religious bore his name, approved as Celestines by Urban IV in 1264. In July 1294 his solitude was broken by election at Perugia, coronation at Aquila on 29 August, and abdication at Naples on 13 December. He died a prisoner in the castle of Fumone on 19 May 1296, after Boniface VIII dissolved the Spiritual Franciscans who had used his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement V, born Bertrand de Got at Villandraut in Gascony in 1264, was elected on 5 June 1305 after an eleven-month conclave split between French and Italian cardinals. Ten of fifteen cardinals, mostly Italian, chose him. Villani's tale of a secret bargain with Philip the Fair in the forest of Saint-Jean-d'Angély is, the entry insists, quite unhistorical, though some understanding with the French king is likely.

As Archbishop of Bordeaux he was a subject of England's king yet a lifelong friend of Philip, while staying faithful to Boniface VIII. The cardinals begged him to come to Perugia and Rome for coronation, but he summoned them to Lyons, where he was crowned on 14 November 1305 before Philip in great pomp. A falling wall threw him from his horse in the procession, killing a brother and the aged Cardinal Orsini and losing the tiara's great carbuncle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory V, born Bruno about 970, was the first German pope, consecrated on 3 May 996. On John XV's death the Romans asked Otto III to name his choice, and Otto named his chaplain and kinsman Bruno, son of Duke Otto of Carinthia and Judith. Already distinguished for learning, above all for the dialects that would grow into modern European languages, Bruno was, despite a hasty temper, a worthy candidate.

One of his first acts was to crown Otto emperor on 21 May 996. Pope and emperor acted in full harmony, holding a synod that restored Arnulf to Reims and condemned Gerbert, the future Sylvester II, as an intruder. When Otto left Rome, the turbulent noble Crescentius rose and drove Gregory north. Crescentius set up the antipope John XVI, whom Otto's troops later captured, mutilated, and degraded before pope and emperor in 998.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent V, Petrus of Tarentaise, born about 1225, won election at Arezzo 21 January 1276 and died at Rome 22 June 1276, the first Dominican pope. His province was certainly Tarentaise on the upper Isère, his birthplace probably Champagny. He entered the Dominicans at sixteen, took his master of sacred theology at Paris in 1259, and earned renown as a teacher, hailed the most famous doctor.

He led his order in France as provincial, then took Lyons as archbishop in 1272 and Ostia as Cardinal-Bishop in 1273. At Lyons's Second Council in 1274 he gave two sermons and spoke Saint Bonaventure's funeral oration. Gregory X's close adviser, he followed him with a peaceable policy. He made peace between Italy's Guelphs and Ghibellines and between Pisa and Lucca. He brokered between Rudolf of Habsburg and Charles of Anjou and laboured to firm up the Greeks' union with Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-v:
Pope John V, a Syrian, son of Cyriacus, ruled from 685 to 686 and died 2 August 686. As deacon he spoke for the Apostolic See at the Sixth Ecumenical Council. He came back to Rome in July 682 bearing the synod's official papers. Emperor Constantine Pogonatus liked him so well that the emperor cut taxes on papal estates in Sicily and Calabria and lightened the Church's fiscal load overall.

His biographer praises his vigour, learning, and moderation warmly, qualities that no doubt won him election in Saint John Lateran's basilica. Constantine Pogonatus had ended the wait for imperial confirmation, so John went straight to the Lateran palace as pope. Consecration followed about 23 July 685, and his reign ran a little over a year. In that short time he gave 1,900 solidi to clergy and deaconries for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-v:
Leo V was a priest from Priapi near Ardea. He served a church outside Rome. He probably held the papacy for about a month in August 903. Lists of the time call him a priest from outside the city. A writer of the time praised his godly life. Almost nothing is known about his election or his reign.

His one recorded act was a bull freeing the canons of Bologna from taxes. Christopher, cardinal-priest of St Damasus, seized him and threw him into prison. There he likely died naturally. One account says Sergius III had both imprisoned popes killed. The entry lays out what can and cannot be known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-martin-v:
Oddone Colonna was born at Genazzano in 1368. He trained at Perugia. He rose through papal offices. He deserted Gregory XII. He took part in electing antipopes at Pisa. The Council of Constance chose him unanimously on 11 November 1417. He was ordained deacon, priest, and bishop within three days. He was crowned at Constance ten days later.

Martin ended the Western Schism. He won over John XXIII and the successors of Benedict XIII. He struck separate concordats, or agreements, with Germany, France, England, Spain, and probably Italy. Then he set out for a ruined, famine-struck Rome. The entry follows his rebuilding of papal rule. It ends with his death in February 1431.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas:
Tommaso Parentucelli was born at Sarzana in 1397. His father was a poor physician. Parentucelli lost his father young. He left Bologna unfinished. He tutored Florentine families. He befriended leading humanists. He took a theology degree in 1422. He spent twenty years serving Bishop Albergati of Bologna. He fed a passion for books and building. He shone at the Council of Florence in debate with Greek bishops.

As pope he secured papal rights over bishoprics and benefices. He did so through the Concordat of Vienna in 1448. He won the submission of the last antipope, Felix V. He marked the end of the schism with a great Jubilee in 1450. Plague scattered the pilgrims and drove him from Rome for a time. He returned to receive German princes and prelates. He died there in March 1455.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-v:
Camillo Borghese was born at Rome in 1550. His family came from Siena and claimed St Catherine as a relative. Unrest drove them from Siena to Rome. Camillo studied law at Perugia and Padua, growing into a canonist of marked ability. Clement VIII made him cardinal in 1596, and he became Cardinal-Vicar of Rome.

On Leo XI's death all eyes turned to him, and he took the throne without engagement or obligation. His legal training showed in all he did. He ruled from the decretals, not diplomacy. He held every right claimed by his predecessors inviolate. His first public act sent absentee prelates and cardinals home to their sees. Trent had called episcopal absence a grave sin. He soon fell into controversy with Italian cities over church rights. The entry follows his stern reign to his death in January 1621.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sixtus-v:
Felice Peretti was born at Grottamare near Montalto in 1521. His Dalmatian family had fled Turkish devastation in Illyria. His father was a gardener, and Felice is said to have herded swine as a boy. At nine he joined Montalto's Minorite convent, where his uncle lived as a friar. He became a novice at twelve and was ordained at Siena in 1547. He won fame as a preacher at Rome in 1552.

Pius IV made him counsellor to the Venetian Inquisition, but his zeal got him recalled in 1560. Elected on 24 April 1585 and crowned on 1 May, he economized ruthlessly except on building. He raised taxes, sold offices, and extended public loans. He built the Lateran Palace, finished the Quirinal, and founded a hospice for the poor. Before his death he had stored three million gold scudi and one million six hundred thousand silver in Sant' Angelo. He died on 27 August 1590.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-pius-:
Michele Ghisleri was born at Bosco near Alessandria in 1504 to a poor but noble family. The Dominicans of Voghera took him in and schooled him in solid, austere devotion. He joined the order, took ordination in 1528, and spent sixteen years teaching theology and philosophy. He served as master of novices and prior of several houses, fasting, doing penance, and spending nights in meditation and prayer.

Paul IV made him bishop of Sutri in 1556, then inquisitor in Milan and Lombardy, and in 1557 cardinal and inquisitor general for all Christendom. At Mondovì from 1559 he restored faith and discipline battered by Piedmont's wars. He blocked Pius IV from admitting thirteen-year-old Ferdinand de' Medici to the Sacred College. He defeated Maximilian II's plan to end clerical celibacy. He was elected on 7 January 1566 and died on 1 May 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Stephen, son of Marinus, reigned from 816 to 817 and died on 24 January 817. He came from the noble Roman family that gave two other popes to the church. Hadrian I and Leo III patronized his youth; Leo made him deacon. Celebrated for virtue, he won election and consecration at once after Leo's death, about 22 June 816.

At once he made Romans swear allegiance to Louis the Pious as suzerain and notified the emperor of his election. He then travelled to France, crowned Louis, received splendid presents, and renewed the Frankish-papal pact. In Gaul, Theodulf of Orléans, a chief imperial adviser, received the pallium from him. Returning through Ravenna, he displayed Christ's sandals for veneration and brought home exiles banished under Leo III. St Peter's holds his grave.
criticism-part-4-from-the-works-of-john-:
Reviews and short critical pieces by John Greenleaf Whittier fill this file, part four of the Criticism volume, volume seven of his works. Six heads stand in the contents: Evangeline, Mirth and Medicine, Fame and Glory, Fanaticism, The Poetry of the North, and Criticism.

The first piece hails Longfellow's Evangeline as the American poem British critics had long taunted the country for lacking. Whittier praises its scenes from Nova Scotia to the Gulf of Mexico. Fame and Glory takes up an address by Charles Sumner at Amherst College. Other pieces weigh mirth as medicine and the worth of northern verse. The file shows the Quaker poet at work as a working critic of his peers.
doe-osti-17120056-the-arm-aerosol-optica:
Connor Flynn and three Pacific Northwest National Laboratory colleagues document a data product for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement program. Flynn works at the University of Oklahoma. Report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-211 is dated August 2026. Aerosols, tiny airborne particles, scatter and absorb sunlight. Climate work needs those effects in standard form. The AOP product computes them from raw site instruments.

Inputs come from absorption and scattering instruments at ARM sites. Named correction schemes are applied to the absorption data. Outputs include scattering and absorption coefficients. They also include single scattering albedo. Angstrom exponents describe how effects change with color. Quality checks, file formats, and site coverage are spelled out, so researchers can use the record with confidence.
doe-osti-1763976-helioscope-energy-perfo:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NREL/TP-6A20-78916, issued in February 2026 with Janine Freeman Keith as technical contact, closes out CRADA project CRD-17-00685. The project tested HelioScope, the web-based solar design and performance modeling tool made by Folsom Labs. Banks and cities had hesitated to trust its energy estimates without vetting from a respected laboratory, and Folsom Labs won a Small Business Voucher to get that check done.

HelioScope systems were built with the same specifications and weather-year data used in earlier studies. Its predictions were then compared against measured output from real photovoltaic systems. The same systems were also run through three established tools, the System Advisor Model, PVSyst, and PV*SOL. The comparison shows how closely the newer tool's engine tracks both field data and the older models' results.
doe-osti-2589494-hydrogen-systems-for-pe:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5D00-96451 closes project CRD-21-21941, called HYPER-V. Technical contact Yiyun Yao, working with partner Eaton, studied hydrogen systems that combine electrolyzers, storage tanks, and fuel cells on the power grid. A hydrogen setup can earn value in several stacked ways, if its controls dispatch it well.

Tasks built and refined simulation models for each device, then joined them into layouts matching real uses. Control software for the electrolyzer, first built under an earlier software record, was matured for dispatch decisions. A market task weighed energy market openings and customer demand shapes to set performance targets. The filing frames when hydrogen systems pay: flexible operation across services, rather than one fixed job.
doe-osti-3003994-versatile-amp-intellige:
Kshitiz Gupta of Lawrence Livermore presents a feasibility study, LLNL-TR-2013728, dated November 2025, for project 25-FS-035. The project, called VIBES, aims at biodetection through environmental sensing. The motivating gap is predictive health monitoring: during the COVID-19 pandemic, testing reacted to illness instead of warning ahead of it. A breath-based sensor could flag both known diseases and new threats.

The project built an optical biosensor that analyzes volatile organic compounds in breath, imitating the sense of smell. Thin metal-coated substrates carried small biological recognition elements. With a visible laser readout, the device detected ethanol reliably down to about 2 parts per million, with early detection of acetone below 100 parts per million. Nanostructures on the film amplified the signal, as expected. Several unexpected influences on sensor behavior were logged for the next design round.
doe-osti-3375873-what-is-produced-water-:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2026/5599, dated May 7, 2026, prices the broth that oil and gas wells pump up with their fuel. Five authors wrote it: Kristen E. Fauria, Brandon Sullivan, Alison Fritz, Justin Mackey, and Nick Siefert. Produced water is mostly a disposal cost today. Yet it holds lithium, a prized battery metal, plus other minerals with market value. The study asks what the full load is worth in two big fields, the Marcellus and the Permian Basin.

The method is bookkeeping at scale. Each mineral's share in the water is priced from the 2025 USGS commodity tables. A molar mass fix turns compound prices into element prices. The team picks base product forms, the least-processed goods that could be sold. They grant that the pick is part judgment, since some recovery tech is still young.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DollahiteVernon:
Patrolman Vernon V. Dollahite of Shelby County was interviewed by the FBI on April 13, 1968. Memphis police and Special Agent Franklin L. Johnson took part. Nine days earlier, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. had been shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, and officers across the area were accounting for their movements.

Dollahite re-enacted what he had done on April 4, the day of the shooting. Interviews of this kind built the investigation's timeline, placing each officer at each hour. His statement preserves one patrolman's part in that record, fixed while memories were still fresh.
in-the-ranks-of-the-c-i-v:
Erskine Childers served as a driver with the City of London Imperial Volunteers battery in South Africa. His diary, In the Ranks of the C.I.V., was published in 1900. He was a clerk in the House of Commons who shipped on the Montfort. Chapters move from Capetown to Bloemfontein and Pretoria.

A shell bursts beside his team and chips his mare's nose in one action. The veldt burns in thin lines of flame as they trot through. Hospital, Warmbad, and the road south close the diary. Childers writes plainly of horses, guns, and daily war work.
king-henry-v:
King Henry V, by William Shakespeare, begins with a Prologue who asks for a muse of fire. He wishes for a kingdom as a stage and princes as actors. Warlike Harry should then appear like Mars, the god of war. Famine, sword, and fire would crouch at his heels for work.

The Prologue admits the small theatre cannot hold the fields of France. He asks the crowd to imagine armies, horses, and Agincourt instead. Two mighty monarchies, he says, are parted by a narrow ocean. Then Canterbury and Ely enter to discuss a bill from the last reign. Their talk turns grand war talk toward church business and law.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-v:
Book Five of Leila, dated 1838, opens with the great battle. Dawn comes slowly after an awful night. Moors on Granada's battlements watch Ferdinand's whole army march.

The Spanish host moves toward the city walls at last. Wrecks of a blackened camp mark the road of war. Leila's story reaches its crisis amid that assault. Love, faith, and family claims must all be settled. Lytton closes his Granada romance with the fall of Moorish Spain. The Alhambra's fate hangs over every battlefield scene. Lytton ends with loss on the winning side too.
macmillan-s-reading-books-book-v:
Macmillan's Reading Books, Book V, is a school reader for Standard V pupils. Its preface explains the aim of the whole series. The books give a systematic course for schools under state inspection. English rules required fluent reading and seventy-five lines of poetry learned by heart.

The Scotch code asked for three hundred lines of new poetry repeated. Meaning, allusions, and word roots had to be known, not just sounds. Parsing and sentence analysis fill out the higher work. Such readers trained generations of British schoolchildren. They joined good literature to strict grammar drill. Book V shows Victorian schooling at its most earnest and exact.
nasa-tm-19680006060-evaluation-of-direct:
K. E. Demorest and A. F. Whitaker, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this memorandum on November 24, 1967. Numbered TM X-53675, it evaluates direct current motors in vacuum. Motors that run happily in air can fail in space, where no air cools them or carries away wear products. Their materials therefore need testing under realistic conditions.

Special materials were chosen for small motors of one-sixth horsepower and worked into the bearing retainers, brushes, and insulation system. The motors then ran in a simulated space environment while component temperatures were monitored. Power output and the torque needed to turn a generator load were recorded throughout. In general, the authors conclude, motor materials are now available that will let direct current motors, open directly to the space environment, operate reliably.
nasa-tm-19700015780-apollo-10-as-505-apo:
Marshall Space Flight Center laboratories prepared this technical summary on May 1, 1969. It covers the Apollo 10 space vehicle, called AS-505, built around the Saturn 5 rocket. Apollo 10 was the dress rehearsal flight for the first Moon landing.

The summary gives a brief, clear description of the whole vehicle. Where needed, it adds related facts to make the picture complete. Where a point needs it, the summary adds related information for clarity. It was not meant to define the vehicle in full detail. Its readers were staff who needed a quick, sound grasp of the craft and its parts before the mission flew.
nasa-tm-19720017951-nasa-balloon-aircraf:
NASA Balloon: Aircraft Ranging, Data and Voice Experiment is a May 1972 report on air traffic control trials. It runs to sixty-nine pages, and its lead author's name is poorly rendered in the scan. High balloons stood in for a satellite during the tests. The concepts under trial were proposed for the ATS-F satellite's planned air traffic control experiment.

The tests ran in September 1971 at Aire-sur-l'Adour in France, with ground stations, balloon platforms, and aircraft supplied by the European Space Research Organization. One ground simulation and two aircraft flights at low elevation angles were conducted at L-band. Even under heavy interference, voice communications and side-tone ranging performed well. The data channels, however, suffered high bit errors that produced false commands, and the report closes with recommendations for improving the equipment.
salem-witchcraft-volumes-i-and-ii-with-a: Charles W. Upham wrote Salem Witchcraft, in Volumes I and II, with an account of Salem Village and a history of opinions on witchcraft and kindred subjects. A note states that the work was originally published in 1867, and the printing shown here is a fourth printing of 1969 from Frederick Ungar Publishing in New York. The contents divide Volume I into a preface, maps and pictures, a general index, an introduction, Part First on Salem Village, and Part Second on witchcraft.
tales-from-many-sources-vol-v:
Tales from Many Sources, Volume V, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1886, is an anthology of stories gathered from magazines and named authors. Its contents open with Lob Lie-by-the-Fire by Juliana H. Ewing, a tale of the lubber-fiend.

Ewing's introduction explains the creature Lob. He is a rough kind of brownie or house elf. He is said to haunt some north-country homesteads. He does the farm laborers' work overnight. His wages are no grander than a cream bowl duly set. Wild Jack and Out of Season come from Temple Bar, Mr. Josiah Smith's Balloon Voyage from Belgravia, and named tales by Mrs. Forrester, Mary Frances Peard, and A. Mary F. Robinson fill the volume. Such sets carried magazine fiction into book form for family reading.
the-agamemnon-of-aeschylus-translated-in: Aeschylus wrote the Agamemnon. Gilbert Murray rendered it into English rhyming verse. Murray was Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford. His notes support the text. George Allen and Unwin of London printed this tenth-thousand copy. The cast list names Agamemnon first. He is king of Argos and Mycenae. He heads the Greek armies at Troy. His wife Clytemnestra stands next. Her lover Aigisthos follows. Cassandra, Priam's daughter and prophetess, closes the list. She is now Agamemnon's slave.
the-life-and-adventures-of-robinson-crus:
Daniel Defoe novel of Robinson Crusoe of York appears here in volume one of a two volume London edition of 1812. A life of De Foe stands before the tale, matching the biography printed in the 1808 edition record held here. It gives his London birth about 1663 to a butcher father in Cripplegate.

Schooling at Newington, an early pamphlet, and service in the Monmouth rising fill the opening pages. The title page promises Crusoe travels round three parts of the globe, written by himself. Shipwreck, solitude, and Friday wait beyond the long author biography.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-:
Gilbert Parker's Weavers continues in this volume record with book two, chapters five to fourteen. A contents list precedes chapter five, The Wider Way, which is built from a letter. Faith Claridge writes from Hamley to her brother David in Cairo, in the Quaker thee-and-thou of their people, asking whether he still loves the village that gave him sour bread.

Faith reports that Jasper Kimber, the man David struck at the public-house, followed a lass to London and begged her to marry him. She refused, then relented conditionally: three years sober and hard-working would earn him an answer. Kimber, laid up with fever, opened his whole mind to Faith and grew thankful for David's knocks. Chapter V of the 1947 report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine weighs what could be done about the land's future. UNSCOP had toured Palestine and heard Jews and Arabs state rival claims. Britain was ending its mandate, and a choice could not be put off.

The chapter tests the main options against the facts the panel had gathered. It looks at partition, a single shared state, and other plans for rule. It sets out the gains and costs of each path. This groundwork leads straight to the rival plans that close the report.
